components.name: End User (Browser)
components.description: Employee or attacker using a browser to reach the RetireEasy/NodeGoat web application over HTTP on port 4000.

components.name: NodeGoat Express Server
components.description: Express 4 application (server.js) that serves all routes, renders Swig/consolidate HTML templates, manages express-session sessions and connects to MongoDB. Helmet, csurf and dont-sniff-mimetype are dependencies but their use is commented out in server.js.
assets: SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers

components.name: Session/Auth Handler
components.description: SessionHandler implements login, signup, logout and the isLoggedInMiddleware / isAdminUserMiddleware guards based on req.session.userId; passwords are stored in plaintext in addUser with the bcrypt hashing fix commented out.

components.name: Profile Handler
components.description: Handles GET/POST /profile; reads and writes first name, last name, SSN, date of birth, address, bank account and bank routing number, validating routing number with a backtracking-prone regex and HTML-encoding website output with ESAPI.

components.name: Contributions Handler
components.description: Handles GET/POST /contributions; passes request body fields preTax, afterTax and roth directly to eval() before persisting contribution percentages for the session user.

components.name: Allocations Handler
components.description: Handles GET /allocations/:userId; takes the target userId from the URL parameter rather than the session and passes an unvalidated threshold query value into the allocations lookup.

components.name: Benefits Handler
components.description: Handles GET/POST /benefits, listing all non-admin users and updating their benefit start dates; mounted with only isLoggedIn, with the isAdmin role middleware left commented out in app/routes/index.js.

components.name: Memos Handler
components.description: Handles GET/POST /memos; stores the raw memo body in MongoDB and renders all memos to every logged-in user through the marked Markdown filter.

components.name: Research Handler
components.description: Handles GET /research; concatenates the client-supplied url and symbol query parameters and issues a server-side HTTP request with needle, writing the fetched body back into the response.

components.name: Learn Redirect Endpoint
components.description: GET /learn handler defined inline in app/routes/index.js that redirects the browser to whatever URL is supplied in the url query string without validation.

components.name: Tutorial Router
components.description: Unauthenticated Express router serving static tutorial pages at /tutorial and /tutorial/<page> describing the intentional vulnerabilities, including default account credentials.

components.name: MongoDB (nodegoat)
components.description: MongoDB 4.4 instance holding users, allocations, contributions and memos collections; reached via the MONGODB_URI connection string, defaulting to mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat and mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat in docker-compose.

components.name: Database Reset Seeder
components.description: artifacts/db-reset.js script run at container start and via npm run db:seed; drops collections and inserts fixed admin and user accounts with hardcoded passwords.

components.name: External Stock Quote Site
components.description: Third-party site (default https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/ supplied as a hidden form field) that the research handler fetches server-side; the destination is fully attacker-controllable via the url parameter.

components.name: GitHub Actions CI
components.description: CI workflows that check out the repository, install dependencies, start MongoDB in Docker and run Cypress end-to-end tests and jshint linting.

components.name: mongodb datastore
components.description: Datastore detected from mongodb in package.json.

components.name: web (compose)
components.description: Deployment target (compose) web defined in docker-compose.yml, ports 4000.

components.name: Dockerfile (dockerfile)
components.description: Deployment target (dockerfile) Dockerfile defined in Dockerfile, ports 4000.

components.description: Deployment target (github_actions) e2e-test.yml:e2e-test defined in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml.

trustBoundaries.name: Public internet to NodeGoat web server
trustBoundaries.description: Browser traffic reaches the Express application on port 4000 over plain HTTP (the HTTPS setup in server.js is commented out), crossing from untrusted clients into server-side request handling.

trustBoundaries.name: Unauthenticated to authenticated/administrative area
trustBoundaries.description: isLoggedInMiddleware separates unauthenticated routes (/, /login, /signup, /logout, /tutorial) from session-bearing routes; the admin-only benefits functions sit behind the same check with no role middleware.

trustBoundaries.name: Application to MongoDB

threats.title: MongoDB connection from the Allocations Handler is unauthenticated and unencrypted on the container network
threats.asset: the nodegoat MongoDB collections, including plaintext user passwords and SSN/bank details
threats.attackScenario: config/env/all.js:3 and docker-compose.yml:8 point the app at mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat with no credentials and no TLS options, so anyone who obtains a foothold on the compose network connects to mongo:27017 directly, or sniffs the wire-protocol traffic carrying the allocations and users queries, and reads or rewrites the users collection where app/data/user-dao.js:25 stores the password verbatim.
assumptions: An attacker can reach the container network, for example through another compromised service or a misconfigured host port.
The application connects to MongoDB without authentication or with excessive privileges, as shown in the default docker-compose configuration.
The mongo:4.4 service is started without --auth and without TLS, as the credential-free URI in docker-compose.yml implies.
threats.impactReason: Direct database access exposes and allows tampering with plaintext passwords, SSN and bank routing fields, allocations, contributions and memos.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a position on the container network rather than an internet-facing request, but no authentication stands in the way once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection used by the DAOs.
steps: Start the mongo service in docker-compose.yml with --auth and create a dedicated application user restricted to the nodegoat database.
Put credentials and tls=true into MONGODB_URI rather than the credential-free default in config/env/all.js:3.
Keep port 27017 unpublished and restrict it to the application service on the compose network.

threats.title: Unvalidated threshold query value flows into the allocations MongoDB lookup
threats.asset: other users' asset allocation records
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/allocations.js:19-23 takes `threshold` straight from req.query and passes it into allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold, where it becomes part of the search criteria against the allocations collection; an attacker submits GET /allocations/1?threshold[$gt]= or a crafted operator string in the free-text `threshold` field of app/views/allocations.html:22 to change the query's selector and return allocation rows the filter was meant to exclude.
assumptions: The threshold value reaches the MongoDB query selector without being coerced to a number or otherwise validated in app/data/allocations-dao.js (the excerpt ends before the searchCriteria body).
threats.impactReason: Query manipulation returns allocation records outside the intended filter, but the collection reached is limited to allocations.
threats.likelihoodReason: The threshold parameter is attacker-controlled on a route any authenticated user can call, and the HTML input is plain text with the numeric-validation fix commented out.

mitigation.summary: Validate and coerce threshold to an integer before it is used in the query.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js parse threshold with parseInt and reject values outside 0-99 before calling getByUserIdAndThreshold.
In app/data/allocations-dao.js build the selector from the parsed number only, never from the raw request value.
Restore the numeric input at app/views/allocations.html:21 as defence in depth.

threats.title: Unbounded allocations query from the handler can be used to exhaust database resources
threats.asset: availability of the allocations lookup and the MongoDB instance
threats.attackScenario: getByUserIdAndThreshold is called from app/routes/allocations.js:23 with no result limit and no rate limiting in front of GET /allocations/:userId, so an attacker loops requests with varying :userId and threshold values to force repeated unindexed scans of the allocations collection over the MongoDB wire connection until the database saturates and the route stops responding for other users.
assumptions: No rate limiting or connection throttling is applied in front of the /allocations route.
The allocations collection query is not bounded by a limit or served by an index on userId and stocks.
threats.impactReason: Saturating the shared MongoDB instance degrades every feature backed by it, not just allocations.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated account can issue the requests in a loop with no throttle in the path.

mitigation.summary: Bound and throttle the allocations lookup.
steps: Apply a limit() to the cursor in app/data/allocations-dao.js getByUserIdAndThreshold.
Add an index on allocations.userId and reject non-numeric threshold values early in app/routes/allocations.js.
Add express rate limiting to the /allocations routes registered in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: No per-request audit trail for cross-user allocation reads
threats.asset: audit record of who read which user's allocations
threats.attackScenario: The GET /allocations/:userId handler in app/routes/allocations.js renders the allocations view without recording the session identity alongside the requested userId, so an attacker who walks ids to harvest other users' allocations leaves no record tying the reads to their account and can deny having performed them.
assumptions: No upstream access logging records the authenticated session identity together with the requested :userId path parameter.
threats.impactReason: Loss of accountability hinders incident response but does not by itself disclose or alter data.
threats.likelihoodReason: The absence of logging is passive and applies to every request on a route any authenticated user can reach.

mitigation.summary: Log session identity and requested userId for allocation reads.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js log req.session.userId, req.params.userId and the threshold value on each displayAllocations call.
Emit a distinct warning entry when req.session.userId differs from req.params.userId.

threats.title: IDOR on GET /allocations/:userId exposes other users' allocation records
threats.asset: other users' asset allocation records and names
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/allocations.js:16-18 reads userId from req.params instead of req.session (the session-based fix is commented out at lines 13-15) and no ownership or role check runs before the handler, so an attacker logs in with any account and requests GET /allocations/1, /allocations/2 and so on to read every other user's stocks/funds/bonds percentages along with their first and last names rendered by app/views/allocations.html.
threats.impactReason: Every user's allocation record and name is enumerable one sequential integer id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered, authenticated user reaches the route and user ids are sequential integers generated by getNextSequence.

mitigation.summary: Derive the target userId from the session rather than the URL parameter.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js replace `const { userId } = req.params;` with `const { userId } = req.session;` as the commented fix at lines 13-15 indicates.
If a URL parameter must remain, compare req.params.userId against req.session.userId and return 404 when they differ.
Add an ownership-check middleware in app/routes/index.js for the /allocations/:userId route.

threats.title: Credentials and session cookie on the allocations request can be read on the wire if the app is served over plain HTTP
threats.asset: session cookie
threats.attackScenario: The End User (Browser) -> Allocations Handler flow is described as HTTP on port 4000, so an attacker on the same office wifi captures the GET /allocations/:userId request, lifts the session cookie from the Cookie header, and replays it to read that user's allocation records.
assumptions: No TLS termination is in place, so traffic including credentials and sensitive personal data is sent over plain HTTP.
The application is reached directly over http://host:4000 with no TLS-terminating proxy in front of it.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie gives full authenticated access to the victim's account and, via the userId path parameter, to other users' allocations.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network adjacency to the victim, but no application-level exploit; every allocations request carries the cookie. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Terminate TLS in front of the app and mark session cookies secure.
steps: Serve the application behind HTTPS and redirect plain HTTP requests on port 4000.
Set `secure: true` and `httpOnly: true` on the express session cookie configuration.
Add HSTS response headers so browsers never retry over plain HTTP.

threats.title: Insecure direct object reference on GET /allocations/:userId exposes other employees' allocations
threats.asset: other users' asset allocation records and names
threats.attackScenario: AllocationsHandler.displayAllocations at app/routes/allocations.js:16 takes userId from req.params instead of req.session (the session-based fix is commented out at lines 12-15) and passes it straight to allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold, so any logged-in employee changes the path from /allocations/3 to /allocations/1 and the allocations.html view renders another user's stocks, funds, bonds, firstName and lastName.
threats.impactReason: Every user's retirement allocation records and names can be enumerated one small integer id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered or existing authenticated user reaches the route by editing the URL; no tooling or special position is required.

mitigation.summary: Derive the user id from the session rather than the URL path, and enforce an ownership/role check.
steps: Restore the commented-out fix in app/routes/allocations.js: use `const { userId } = req.session;` instead of `req.params`.
If admin access to other users' allocations is required, gate the req.params branch on an explicit isAdmin check before calling allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold.
Return 404 for ids the caller may not view so the endpoint does not confirm which user ids exist.

threats.title: Unvalidated threshold query parameter reaches the allocations Mongo query
threats.asset: other users' asset allocation records
threats.attackScenario: The allocations search form at app/views/allocations.html:22 submits `threshold` as a free-text input (the numeric 0-99 input is commented out at lines 17-21) and app/routes/allocations.js:19-23 forwards req.query.threshold unvalidated into allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold, so an attacker requests GET /allocations/1?threshold=<JavaScript expression or operator payload> to alter the search criteria and pull allocation documents beyond the intended filter.
assumptions: getByUserIdAndThreshold builds its search criteria from the raw threshold string without casting or sanitising it, as the commented-out note in app/views/allocations.html indicates the server-side fix in allocations-dao.js was also left unapplied.
threats.impactReason: A crafted threshold can subvert the query filter and return allocation records the caller should not see, or stall the database.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is attacker-controlled on a GET URL reachable by any authenticated user, and the front-end validation that would constrain it is disabled.

mitigation.summary: Validate and coerce the threshold to an integer before it reaches the query.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js, parse threshold with parseInt and reject values outside 0-99 with a 400 response before calling the DAO.
Build the search criteria in app/data/allocations-dao.js from the parsed number only, never from the raw string.
Re-enable the numeric input at app/views/allocations.html:21 for defence in depth.

threats.title: Session cookie forgery and hijacking because the session/auth check trusts an unprotected req.session.userId
threats.asset: session identifiers and the authenticated user's SSN, date of birth and bank account details
threats.attackScenario: The isLoggedInMiddleware at app/routes/session.js:36 authorises a request purely on the presence of req.session.userId, and server.js sets up express-session with a cookieSecret loaded from config while the HTTPS server block at server.js:18-28 is commented out, so an attacker on the same network captures the connect.sid cookie from a plaintext request to /dashboard and replays it to reach /profile and /allocations as that user.
assumptions: No TLS termination is in place, so traffic including credentials and sensitive personal data is sent over plain HTTP.
The application is served over plain HTTP because the https listener in server.js remains commented out and no TLS terminator is placed in front of it.
The express-session cookie is not marked Secure, so it is transmitted over the cleartext channel.
threats.impactReason: A replayed session identifier gives full access to the victim's profile containing SSN, date of birth and bank account and routing numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Interception requires a network position, but the cleartext default and the presence-only session check make replay trivial once a cookie is seen. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Terminate TLS and harden the express-session cookie and its secret.
steps: Uncomment or replace the https listener in server.js so the app only serves over TLS, and add helmet.hsts().
Configure express-session with cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' } and a maxAge, and call req.session.regenerate() on successful login in app/routes/session.js.
Load cookieSecret from an environment variable rather than a committed config value.

threats.title: Session fixation and forged state via the in-process auth check with CSRF protection disabled
threats.asset: user session state and the retirement contribution and allocation data changed by forged requests
threats.attackScenario: csurf is required only in a commented-out line at server.js:7 so no CSRF token is validated before isLoggedInMiddleware hands a request to a protected handler, letting an attacker host a page that auto-submits a form to POST /contributions or POST /profile; the victim's browser attaches the session cookie the auth flow trusts and the victim's contribution percentages or profile fields are rewritten.
assumptions: CSRF protection is not applied to these state-changing routes, leaving them vulnerable to cross-site request forgery.
No CSRF middleware is registered anywhere else in the request pipeline, so state-changing POST routes accept cross-site form submissions.
threats.impactReason: Forged requests can alter contributions, benefits and profile fields of any logged-in victim without the attacker ever seeing the session cookie.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only a logged-in victim visiting an attacker page is required; the POST routes are known and use simple form bodies. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable csurf on all state-changing routes and pair it with SameSite cookies.
steps: Uncomment the csurf require at server.js:7 and app.use(csrf()) after the session middleware.
Emit the token into every Swig form template and reject requests failing validation in app/routes/error.js.
Set cookie.sameSite = 'strict' on the express-session configuration as defence in depth.

threats.title: Unbounded session-checked request handling lets a single client stall the Node process
threats.asset: availability of the authenticated dashboard and profile routes
threats.attackScenario: Every protected request passes through isLoggedInMiddleware at app/routes/session.js:36 and then handlers that query MongoDB, with no rate limiter or request cap in server.js, so an attacker who registers one account loops GET /dashboard and GET /allocations/:userId from many connections and exhausts the single forever-managed Node process and its MongoDB connections.
assumptions: No reverse proxy or rate-limiting middleware is deployed in front of the container exposed on port 4000 by docker-compose.yml.
The application connects to MongoDB without authentication or with excessive privileges, as shown in the default docker-compose configuration.
threats.impactReason: The Procfile runs a single Node process, so saturation takes the whole application offline for all users.
threats.likelihoodReason: Registration is open and the protected routes are cheap to call in bulk once a session exists. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Add request rate limiting and connection limits in front of the session-checked routes.
steps: Register a rate-limiting middleware in server.js before routes are mounted, keyed on session id and source IP.
Bound the MongoDB driver pool size in the MongoClient.connect options in server.js.
Run more than one process or place a reverse proxy with connection limits in front of the container in docker-compose.yml.

threats.title: Unvalidated redirect on GET /learn sends users to an attacker-controlled login page
threats.asset: login credentials and session cookie of the redirected user
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70-72 passes req.query.url straight into res.redirect with no allow-list, so an attacker mails a logged-in employee a link to /learn?url=https://retire-easy-login.example and the trusted NodeGoat origin bounces the victim to a cloned login page that harvests their credentials.
assumptions: No upstream middleware rewrites or filters the url query parameter before the handler runs.
threats.impactReason: Credential phishing borrowing the application's own domain leads to account takeover, though no data is read directly from the server.
threats.likelihoodReason: The redirect target is taken verbatim from the query string and the route needs only an authenticated session to reach.

mitigation.summary: Restrict /learn redirects to a fixed allow-list of destinations.
steps: Replace res.redirect(req.query.url) in app/routes/index.js:72 with a lookup of req.query.url against a hardcoded map of permitted learning-resource URLs.
Reject or 400 any value not present in the map instead of redirecting.
If arbitrary targets are truly needed, render an interstitial page that shows the destination host before navigation.

threats.title: Missing security response headers on rendered Swig pages allow clickjacking and unrestricted script sources
threats.asset: user session state and rendered profile data in the browser
threats.attackScenario: server.js has helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() and helmet.frameguard() commented out at lines 45-51 and app/views/layout.html sets no CSP meta tag, so an attacker frames /profile on a lookalike page and overlays controls to trick a logged-in employee into submitting a profile update, or loads attacker-hosted script into the rendered page unimpeded by any script-src policy.
assumptions: CSRF protection is not applied to these state-changing routes, leaving them vulnerable to cross-site request forgery.
No reverse proxy adds Content-Security-Policy or X-Frame-Options headers to responses in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Clickjacked profile updates can alter bank details and the absent CSP removes the last defence against injected script in rendered memo and profile content.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires luring an authenticated user to an attacker page, but the framing and script-source restrictions are entirely absent. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Re-enable helmet's frameguard, CSP and MIME-sniffing protections.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require at server.js:10 and the app.use(helmet.frameguard()) and helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() lines in the Fix for A5 block.
Configure a script-src/style-src policy that permits only /vendor assets served by the app.
Re-enable dont-sniff-mimetype and app.disable("x-powered-by") in server.js.

threats.title: Unencrypted HTTP delivery of rendered pages exposes the session cookie and profile data
threats.asset: session cookie and rendered SSN, date of birth and bank account details
threats.attackScenario: server.js creates a plain http server with the https key/cert loading block commented out at lines 18-28 and the helmet.hsts() call commented out at line 54, so an attacker on the same network as a user passively captures the /profile response carrying SSN and bank routing numbers and lifts the express-session cookie from the request header, then replays it to impersonate the victim.
assumptions: No TLS termination is in place, so traffic including credentials and sensitive personal data is sent over plain HTTP.
No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Express server in the deployment described by docker-compose.yml, which publishes port 4000 directly.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie yields full account takeover and the same traffic carries SSN and bank details in clear text.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any shared-network or on-path position suffices and every response on this flow is affected. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark the session cookie secure.
steps: Uncomment the https options block in server.js and create the server with https.createServer(httpsOptions, app), or terminate TLS in a proxy and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Re-enable helmet.hsts() in server.js so browsers refuse plaintext connections.
Set cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' } on the express-session configuration in server.js.

threats.title: Another user's allocations rendered back to any logged-in caller via GET /allocations/:userId
threats.asset: other employees' retirement allocation records and names
threats.attackScenario: GET /allocations/:userId at app/routes/index.js:63 is guarded only by isLoggedIn with no ownership or role check, so an attacker signs up, notes the numeric userId embedded in their own /allocations link in app/views/layout.html:56, and iterates neighbouring ids to have the server render other employees' stock, fund and bond allocations together with their first and last names into the HTML response.
assumptions: No ownership comparison is performed inside allocationsHandler.displayAllocations before the record is rendered.
The application connects to MongoDB without authentication or with excessive privileges, as shown in the default docker-compose configuration.
threats.impactReason: Every employee's allocation record and name becomes readable one sequential id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered account reaches the route and the user ids are small sequential integers generated by getNextSequence. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Scope the allocations lookup to the session's own user id.
steps: In the /allocations/:userId handler, compare req.params.userId against req.session.userId and return 403 (or redirect) when they differ, unless the session user is an admin.
Alternatively drop the :userId parameter and read allocations for req.session.userId only, updating the link in app/views/layout.html:56.
Add the same ownership guard as middleware at app/routes/index.js:63.

threats.title: Swig 1.4.2 arbitrary local file read through template rendering
threats.asset: local server files such as config/env/all.js containing the cookie secret and crypto key
threats.attackScenario: package.json:22 pins swig@^1.4.2, affected by CVE-2023-25345 with no fixed release, and server.js wires swig through consolidate as the view engine for every rendered response, so an attacker who influences a template path or include directive on this flow makes the renderer read an arbitrary file from disk and returns its contents inside the HTML response.
assumptions: At least one rendering path allows attacker-influenced data to reach a template name or include directive.
threats.impactReason: Reading config/env/all.js discloses the cookie secret and crypto key, allowing session forgery and decryption of any encrypted profile fields.
threats.likelihoodReason: The vulnerable library is definitely in use and unpatched, but exploitation needs an attacker-influenced template path which is not demonstrated in the excerpts.

mitigation.summary: Replace the unmaintained swig renderer with a maintained template engine.
steps: Migrate app/views/*.html to a maintained engine such as nunjucks or twig and update the consolidate engine registration in server.js.
Remove the swig dependency from package.json:22.
Ensure no render() call anywhere in app/routes takes its template name from request data.

threats.title: Unauthenticated MongoDB on the benefits-handler to nodegoat flow exposes the whole users collection
threats.asset: users collection contents including plaintext passwords, SSN and bank details
threats.attackScenario: The connection string used for this flow is mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat (docker-compose.yml:8, config/env/all.js:3) with no username, password or TLS parameters, so an attacker who lands on the container network connects to mongo:27017 as an anonymous client, impersonating the Benefits Handler, and reads or rewrites the users collection that benefits-dao.js queries — including password, ssn, bankAcc and bankRouting fields.
assumptions: No TLS is configured on the MongoDB wire protocol connection.
The MongoDB instance is started without authentication enabled, as implied by the credential-free URI in config/env/all.js and docker-compose.yml.
The application connects to MongoDB without authentication or with excessive privileges, as shown in the default docker-compose configuration.
threats.impactReason: The users collection holds plaintext passwords, SSNs and bank account details for every employee, all readable and writable with no credential.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network access to the Mongo port, which is only exposed inside the compose network, but any co-located container or host-level foothold reaches it unauthenticated. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authenticated, TLS-protected MongoDB connections with a least-privilege application user.
steps: Enable MongoDB authentication in docker-compose.yml and create a dedicated application user restricted to the nodegoat database.
Set MONGODB_URI to include those credentials plus tls=true instead of the credential-free default in config/env/all.js:3.
Restrict the mongo service so only the web service can reach port 27017.

threats.title: Unbounded roster read on the benefits flow can be used to exhaust the application
threats.asset: availability of the benefits page and the MongoDB nodegoat instance
threats.attackScenario: getAllNonAdminUsers at app/data/benefits-dao.js:15 issues an unfiltered find({isAdmin:{$ne:true}}).toArray() with no limit or pagination and is invoked on every GET /benefits and again after every POST /benefits, so a logged-in attacker loops POST /benefits requests to force repeated full-collection scans and materialisation of the entire users collection into memory until the Node process and Mongo are saturated.
assumptions: No rate limiting is applied in front of the /benefits routes.
threats.impactReason: Repeated full-collection reads degrade or stall both the Node process and the shared MongoDB instance used by all other handlers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user can issue the requests, but the impact scales with collection size and requires sustained traffic.

mitigation.summary: Paginate the roster query and rate limit the benefits routes.
steps: Add skip/limit paging to usersCol.find in app/data/benefits-dao.js:15 and project only the fields benefits.html renders.
Apply a request rate limiter to the GET and POST /benefits routes in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: Any logged-in employee can view and rewrite every colleague's benefit start date via /benefits
threats.asset: employee roster and benefit start dates for all non-admin users
threats.attackScenario: GET /benefits (app/routes/index.js:55) and POST /benefits (app/routes/index.js:56) are mounted with only isLoggedIn and the handler in app/routes/benefits.js renders the full non-admin roster with a hardcoded user:{isAdmin:true} context, so a non-privileged employee signs in, browses to /benefits to read every colleague's employee id, first name, last name and benefitStartDate, then submits POST /benefits with userId set to any other employee's _id and an arbitrary benefitStartDate, which benefits-dao.js:23 writes straight into the users collection.
assumptions: The isAdmin role middleware is not applied to /benefits anywhere upstream of app/routes/index.js.
threats.impactReason: The entire non-admin employee roster is disclosed and any employee's benefit start date can be silently altered, affecting payroll/benefits eligibility.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered or ordinary account reaches the route directly; no special position or exploit is required.

mitigation.summary: Enforce admin authorization on both /benefits routes and scope updates server-side.
steps: Re-enable the isAdmin role middleware on the GET and POST /benefits routes in app/routes/index.js instead of relying on isLoggedIn alone.
Remove the hardcoded user:{isAdmin:true} object from displayBenefits and updateBenefits in app/routes/benefits.js and pass the real session user.
Have updateBenefits re-check the session user's admin flag before calling benefitsDAO.updateBenefits.

threats.title: Unvalidated benefitStartDate and userId written to the users collection from POST /benefits
threats.asset: benefit start dates in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: updateBenefits in app/routes/benefits.js:29 destructures userId and benefitStartDate straight from req.body and passes them to benefitsDAO.updateBenefits, which at app/data/benefits-dao.js:23 sets benefitStartDate to the raw value with no format or range check, so an attacker posts benefitStartDate= or a nonsense date for an arbitrary userId and corrupts the stored roster data that benefits.html later renders.
assumptions: No validation middleware sanitises req.body before the benefits handler runs.
threats.impactReason: Stored benefit dates for any employee can be set to arbitrary strings, corrupting benefits records and seeding stored content into the benefits view.
threats.likelihoodReason: The POST body is fully attacker-controlled and the route only requires a logged-in session.

mitigation.summary: Validate userId and benefitStartDate before persisting.
steps: Reject requests in app/routes/benefits.js where userId is not a positive integer after parseInt.
Validate benefitStartDate against a strict YYYY-MM-DD pattern and a sane date range before calling benefitsDAO.updateBenefits.
Move the parseInt/date coercion into app/data/benefits-dao.js so the DAO never writes a raw request string.

threats.title: Benefit changes are not attributable to the acting user
threats.asset: audit trail for benefit start date changes
threats.attackScenario: benefitsDAO.updateBenefits at app/data/benefits-dao.js:23 logs only the literal string "Updated benefits" and records no acting session user, target userId or previous value, so an employee who alters a colleague's benefitStartDate through POST /benefits leaves nothing that ties the change to their account and can deny having made it.
assumptions: No external audit logging middleware records request bodies or session identities for /benefits.
threats.impactReason: Unauthorised benefit modifications cannot be attributed or reconstructed during an investigation.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every write through this route is unattributed by default; no attacker effort is needed to achieve deniability.

mitigation.summary: Record an attributable audit entry for each benefits update.
steps: In app/routes/benefits.js updateBenefits, log the session user id, target userId, old and new benefitStartDate before calling the DAO.
Persist the audit entry to a dedicated collection rather than console.log in app/data/benefits-dao.js.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery on POST /benefits changes another employee's benefit start date
threats.asset: benefit start dates in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: The benefits form at app/views/benefits.html:54 posts userId and benefitStartDate to /benefits with no anti-CSRF token, and csurf is left commented out at server.js:7, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form with userId=<victim or other employee id> and benefitStartDate=2099-01-01 to http://<host>/benefits; when a logged-in user visits it the browser attaches the session cookie and benefits-dao.js:23 writes the attacker's date into that employee's record.
assumptions: CSRF protection is not applied to these state-changing routes, leaving them vulnerable to cross-site request forgery.
No CSRF middleware is mounted anywhere in the Express stack in front of the POST /benefits route.
threats.impactReason: Benefit start dates for arbitrary employee ids can be silently rewritten, corrupting HR records without any audit trail in the handler.
threats.likelihoodReason: The route accepts a simple form-encoded POST and requires only that a logged-in user visit an attacker-controlled page; the userId is fully attacker-chosen in the body. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable the already-declared csurf middleware and render its token in the benefits form.
steps: Uncomment the csurf require at server.js:7 and mount `app.use(csrf())` after the session middleware in server.js.
Render `<input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="{{csrftoken}}">` inside the form at app/views/benefits.html:54.
Also apply the commented-out isAdmin middleware shown at app/routes/index.js:57-60 so the route is not reachable by ordinary employees at all.

threats.title: Plain HTTP carries the session cookie and benefits form on the browser-to-server flow
threats.asset: session cookie and the SSN, date of birth and bank account data rendered on authenticated pages
threats.attackScenario: server.js starts the app with the plain `http` module while the HTTPS key/cert loading block at server.js:18-28 is commented out, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi as an employee sniffs the GET /dashboard request, lifts the connect.sid session cookie from the cleartext Cookie header, and replays it to read /profile and /allocations pages containing SSN and bank account numbers, or rewrites the POST /benefits body in transit.
assumptions: No TLS termination is in place, so traffic including credentials and sensitive personal data is sent over plain HTTP.
The application is deployed behind no TLS-terminating proxy, so browser traffic reaches the Express server over plain HTTP as configured in server.js.
threats.impactReason: Session cookie capture yields full account takeover and exposes SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers rendered on authenticated pages.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position (shared Wi-Fi, hostile ISP or proxy), but no application-level defence exists once that position is held. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Terminate TLS for all browser traffic and mark the session cookie Secure and HttpOnly.
steps: Uncomment and complete the https server setup in server.js:18-28 (or place the app behind a TLS-terminating proxy) and stop listening on plain http.
Set `cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' }` on the express-session options in server.js.
Enable helmet.hsts(), already a declared dependency in package.json, so browsers refuse to downgrade.

threats.title: Unvalidated userId in POST /benefits body lets any logged-in user target arbitrary employee records
threats.asset: benefit start dates of other employees in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: POST /benefits at app/routes/index.js:56 runs behind isLoggedIn only, and app/routes/benefits.js:29-35 takes userId straight from req.body into benefitsDAO.updateBenefits, which does `parseInt(userId)` and `$set` at app/data/benefits-dao.js:23-30 with no ownership check or date-format validation, so an ordinary employee replays the form with userId=1 and benefitStartDate set to any string and overwrites another employee's benefit start date.
assumptions: The isLoggedIn middleware does not itself enforce an admin role, so non-admin sessions reach the handler.
threats.impactReason: Any employee record's benefitStartDate can be set to an arbitrary unvalidated value, affecting HR/payroll decisions across the roster.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered or ordinary employee session can craft the POST; the id is a plain integer and the roster is enumerable.

mitigation.summary: Require the admin role on POST /benefits and validate the submitted userId and date.
steps: Apply the isAdmin middleware already available at app/routes/index.js:27 to both /benefits routes, as the commented fix at lines 57-60 shows.
In app/routes/benefits.js:29, reject requests where userId is not a positive integer present in the non-admin roster.
Validate benefitStartDate against an ISO date format before passing it to benefitsDAO.updateBenefits.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn steals session-bearing users from the authenticated flow
threats.asset: login credentials of authenticated employees
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70-72 redirects to req.query.url with no allow-list, so an attacker emails an employee a link to http://<host>/learn?url=https://nodegoat-login.example/ and the trusted application host bounces the authenticated browser to a cloned RetireEasy login page that harvests the employee's credentials.
assumptions: No redirect allow-list is applied in middleware upstream of the /learn handler.
threats.impactReason: Credential phishing laundered through the real application hostname yields account takeover of employee accounts holding SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is directly attacker-controlled and the route needs only a logged-in victim clicking a link.

mitigation.summary: Restrict /learn redirects to a fixed allow-list of destinations.
steps: Replace `res.redirect(req.query.url)` at app/routes/index.js:72 with a lookup of a known key against a hardcoded map of permitted learning-resource URLs.
Reject any value that is not in the map with a 400 instead of redirecting.

threats.title: Any logged-in employee reads another employee's allocations by walking /allocations/:userId
threats.asset: other employees' retirement contribution and allocation data
threats.attackScenario: GET /allocations/:userId at app/routes/index.js:63 is guarded only by isLoggedIn with no ownership or role check, so an employee who sees their own link /allocations/{{userId}} rendered in app/views/layout.html:56 substitutes neighbouring integer ids in the URL and reads other employees' retirement contribution and allocation figures over the same authenticated browser session.
assumptions: Employee ids are sequential integers, as the parseInt-based lookups elsewhere in the app suggest.
The allocations handler does not compare the :userId path parameter against the session user id.
threats.impactReason: The full retirement allocation and contribution picture for every employee is readable one id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered employee reaches the route with a browser address-bar edit; no tooling or special position is required.

mitigation.summary: Scope the allocations lookup to the session's own user id unless the caller is an admin.
steps: In the handler mounted at app/routes/index.js:63, compare req.params.userId with the session user id and return 404 when they differ and the session is not admin.
Alternatively drop the path parameter and derive the user id from the session only, updating the link in app/views/layout.html:56.

threats.title: Unvalidated redirect target on GET /learn reachable over the CI-exercised HTTP flow
threats.asset: user session state (authenticated users redirected to attacker-controlled hosts)
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70-72 passes req.query.url straight to res.redirect with no allow-list or validation, so an attacker sends a logged-in user a link to /learn?url=https://attacker.example/login that leaves the trusted origin and renders a cloned NodeGoat login page to harvest credentials, and the same handler accepts javascript: style targets.
assumptions: No redirect allow-list middleware is applied upstream of the /learn handler.
threats.impactReason: Open redirect from an authenticated page enables convincing credential phishing and can chain into token leakage via the referrer.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is directly attacker-controlled and requires only that the victim be logged in and click a link.

mitigation.summary: Validate the redirect target against an allow-list before calling res.redirect.
steps: Replace `res.redirect(req.query.url)` at app/routes/index.js:72 with a lookup of a named key against a hardcoded map of permitted learning-resource URLs.
Reject or 400 any url value that is not in the map instead of forwarding it.

threats.title: CI drives /allocations/:userId with no ownership check, so the flow exercises and normalises a broken access control path
threats.asset: other users' retirement contribution and allocation data
threats.attackScenario: The CI-driven app instance exposes GET /allocations/:userId at app/routes/index.js:63 behind only isLoggedIn, so any account that reaches the server started by the CI job (or by the same code path in a deployed environment) requests /allocations/2, /allocations/3 and so on and reads other users' allocation and contribution records without any ownership or role check.
assumptions: No ownership comparison of req.params.userId against the session user is performed inside allocationsHandler.displayAllocations.
threats.impactReason: Every user's retirement allocation and contribution figures are enumerable one numeric userId at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Self-signup is open at POST /signup, and the only barrier is being logged in; userIds are small integers.

mitigation.summary: Enforce ownership or admin role on the allocations route.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:63, compare req.params.userId with req.session.userId inside allocationsHandler.displayAllocations and return 404 when they differ.
Add the existing isAdmin middleware as an alternative path for administrative viewing, as already sketched for /benefits at app/routes/index.js:57-60.

threats.title: Unauthenticated MongoDB endpoint lets any process on the network impersonate the Contributions Handler
threats.asset: the nodegoat database contents: users (plaintext passwords, SSN, bank details), contributions, allocations and memos
threats.attackScenario: docker-compose.yml:8 points the app at mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat with no username, password or authSource, so any other container or process able to reach port 27017 on the mongo service connects as an anonymous client indistinguishable from the Contributions Handler and reads or drops the users and contributions collections.
assumptions: Another workload can reach the mongo service port on the shared network.
MongoDB is started without --auth, as implied by the credential-free URI used by the web service.
The application connects to MongoDB without authentication or with excessive privileges, as shown in the default docker-compose configuration.
threats.impactReason: Anonymous access grants full read and write over every collection, including plaintext passwords and SSN/bank data, and allows dropping the database.
threats.likelihoodReason: No credential is needed once network reachability exists, but reachability is limited to the internal compose network. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable MongoDB authentication and give the app a least-privilege user.
steps: Start mongod with --auth in docker-compose.yml and create a nodegoat user limited to the nodegoat database.
Put the credentials into MONGODB_URI via a secret rather than a literal in docker-compose.yml.
Restrict the mongo service so only the web service can reach port 27017.

threats.title: Unencrypted MongoDB wire traffic between the Contributions Handler and the nodegoat database
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords, SSN and bank details, and contribution percentages carried on the MongoDB connection
threats.attackScenario: The connection string in config/env/all.js:3 and docker-compose.yml:8 is a bare mongodb:// URI with no TLS option, so an attacker positioned on the container network between the web service and the mongo service reads the upsert from ContributionsDAO.update and the subsequent userDAO.getUserById reply, which returns user documents whose password field is stored in plaintext (app/data/user-dao.js:25), and can also rewrite the contribution document in flight.
assumptions: An attacker can observe or interpose on the network segment shared by the web and mongo containers.
MongoDB is reached over the URI in config/env/all.js / docker-compose.yml with no TLS layer added at deploy time.
threats.impactReason: The same connection carries user documents containing plaintext passwords, SSNs and bank routing details, all readable and modifiable on the wire.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an attacker already on the internal docker network; mongo is only exposed to linked services.

mitigation.summary: Enable TLS on the MongoDB connection and authenticate the client.
steps: Configure mongod with TLS and change the URI in config/env/all.js to include tls=true plus CA settings.
Add credentials and a dedicated least-privilege user to MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml instead of an unauthenticated connection.
Stop storing plaintext passwords by enabling the bcrypt hashing already imported in app/data/user-dao.js.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery changes another user's contribution percentages
threats.asset: payroll contribution percentages
threats.attackScenario: The contributions form at app/views/contributions.html:46 posts preTax/afterTax/roth to /contributions with no CSRF token field, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits the same form and, when a logged-in employee visits it, their session cookie authorises the update and their payroll percentages are rewritten (and, given the eval() at app/routes/contributions.js:32, arbitrary code is executed on their behalf).
assumptions: CSRF protection is not applied to these state-changing routes, leaving them vulnerable to cross-site request forgery.
The session cookie is sent on cross-site form posts, i.e. no SameSite restriction is applied to it.
threats.impactReason: A forged post both alters payroll data and reaches the eval() sink, so it can execute code in the server under a victim's session.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs a logged-in victim to visit attacker content, but the form requires no token and its fields are fully known. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require a per-session CSRF token on POST /contributions.
steps: Add csurf middleware in the Express app setup and render the token as a hidden input in app/views/contributions.html.
Reject POST /contributions when the token is missing or mismatched.
Set the session cookie to SameSite=Lax.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection via preTax/afterTax/roth on POST /contributions
threats.asset: the Node.js application process and all data it can reach, including plaintext user passwords and SSN/bank details in MongoDB
threats.attackScenario: handleContributionsUpdate passes req.body.preTax, req.body.afterTax and req.body.roth straight to eval() at app/routes/contributions.js:32-34, so an authenticated attacker submits the contributions form with preTax=require('child_process').execSync('cat /etc/passwd').toString() (or a value that connects back to the attacker) and executes arbitrary code inside the NodeGoat process, from which the MongoDB connection in app/data/user-dao.js can be used to dump users including their plaintext passwords.
threats.impactReason: Remote code execution in the application process gives full control of the server and of every collection reachable through the shared db handle, including plaintext passwords, SSNs and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any session user can POST the form field; the payload is a plain string and requires no special position or timing.

mitigation.summary: Stop evaluating request data as code; parse the contribution percentages numerically.
steps: Replace the eval() calls at app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 with the already-commented parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) form.
Reject values that are not integers between 0 and 30 before calling contributionsDAO.update.
Add a regression test posting a JavaScript expression to /contributions and asserting a validation error.

threats.title: Contribution updates are not attributable because no audit record is written
threats.asset: payroll contribution percentages and their change history
threats.attackScenario: ContributionsDAO.update performs an upsert that overwrites the previous preTax/afterTax/roth document for the userId at app/data/contributions-dao.js:28 and only writes 'Updated contributions' to console, so an attacker who has hijacked a session changes another employee's payroll percentages and there is no per-user, timestamped record tying the change to the request.
assumptions: CSRF protection is not applied to these state-changing routes, leaving them vulnerable to cross-site request forgery.
No request or audit logging middleware records the contributions POST body and session user elsewhere in the application.
threats.impactReason: Fraudulent payroll changes cannot be attributed or rolled back because the prior document is overwritten and nothing is logged.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an existing session, but any session user triggering the route leaves no usable trail. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Write an immutable audit entry for each contributions update.
steps: In app/routes/contributions.js handleContributionsUpdate, log the session userId, timestamp, old and new percentages to the application logger.
Change the upsert in app/data/contributions-dao.js to also insert a history document rather than only overwriting the current one.

threats.title: Denial of service by evaluating an infinite loop in the contributions form
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat application to all users
threats.attackScenario: Because req.body.preTax is evaluated as code at app/routes/contributions.js:32, an attacker posts preTax=while(1){} to POST /contributions and blocks the single Node.js event loop, making every other route, including /contributions and login, unresponsive.
assumptions: The application runs as a single Node process without a request timeout or worker restart in front of it.
threats.impactReason: A single request permanently hangs the event loop and takes the whole application offline until it is restarted.
threats.likelihoodReason: The payload is trivial and reachable by any session user through the normal contributions form.

mitigation.summary: Remove eval() so no attacker-supplied string can be executed or loop.
steps: Use parseInt() instead of eval() at app/routes/contributions.js:32-34.
Run the app behind a process manager that restarts unresponsive workers.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery forces a victim's payroll contribution update and eval payload
threats.asset: payroll contribution percentages of the logged-in user
threats.attackScenario: An attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to POST /contributions with preTax/afterTax/roth fields; a logged-in RetireEasy user visiting it has their session cookie attached by the browser, and the request is accepted at app/routes/index.js:52 with only the isLoggedIn check, silently rewriting their payroll percentages and reaching the eval() sink on their behalf.
assumptions: CSRF protection is not applied to these state-changing routes, leaving them vulnerable to cross-site request forgery.
No CSRF token or SameSite cookie protection is applied to the /contributions form POST, so a cross-origin form submission is accepted with the victim's session cookie.
threats.impactReason: The victim's payroll deductions are changed without consent, and the forged request also lands on the eval() sink in the victim's session context.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires luring an authenticated user to an attacker page, but the request itself is a simple HTML form POST with no token to guess. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Add CSRF protection and SameSite cookies to the contributions form flow.
steps: Enable a CSRF middleware (e.g. csurf) in the Express app and emit the token as a hidden field in app/views/contributions.html's form.
Reject POST /contributions at app/routes/index.js:52 when the token is missing or mismatched.
Set the session cookie to SameSite=Lax or Strict in the session configuration.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection via preTax/afterTax/roth on POST /contributions
threats.asset: the Node.js application server process and the MongoDB data it can reach (user records, contributions)
threats.attackScenario: An authenticated user submits the /contributions form with preTax set to a payload such as `require('child_process').execSync('cat /etc/passwd').toString()` or an infinite loop; app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 passes req.body.preTax, req.body.afterTax and req.body.roth straight to eval(), executing the attacker's code in the server process and letting them read the Mongo connection string, dump user documents or hang the single-threaded event loop.
threats.impactReason: eval() with request data is full remote code execution as the application user, exposing every asset the process holds including session secrets and the contributions and users collections.
threats.likelihoodReason: The flow is a plain HTML form POST reachable by any self-registered, logged-in user, and the payload needs no special tooling.

mitigation.summary: Stop evaluating request body values as code; parse the three contribution fields as integers.
steps: Replace the eval() calls at app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 with parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) etc. (the commented-out fix already present at lines 38-40).
Reject any value that is not a finite integer between 0 and 30 before calling contributionsDAO.update.
Add a lint rule (no-eval) so eval() cannot be reintroduced in app/routes.

threats.title: Session cookie and contribution percentages exposed in transit on the POST /contributions flow
threats.asset: session cookie and payroll contribution percentages
threats.attackScenario: An attacker on the same network path as the victim captures the plaintext HTTP POST /contributions request carrying the session cookie and the preTax/afterTax/roth values, then replays the cookie to impersonate the user or rewrites the body to inject an eval payload before it reaches app/routes/contributions.js.
assumptions: No TLS termination is in place, so traffic including credentials and sensitive personal data is sent over plain HTTP.
The browser-to-application flow is served over plain HTTP without HSTS or enforced TLS termination in front of the Express app.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie gives full account takeover and the request body reaches a remote-code-execution sink.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an on-path position such as shared Wi-Fi or a hostile proxy. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enforce HTTPS for all browser traffic and mark the session cookie secure.
steps: Terminate TLS in front of the app and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Set Strict-Transport-Security via helmet in the Express bootstrap.
Set secure: true and httpOnly: true on the session cookie configuration.

threats.title: MongoDB connection string in docker-compose.yml uses no authentication or TLS
threats.asset: the nodegoat MongoDB database contents (user accounts, allocations, memos)
threats.attackScenario: The compose file sets MONGODB_URI to mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat at docker-compose.yml:8 with no username, password or tls option, so an attacker who obtains any foothold on the compose bridge network (for example via the web container exposed on port 4000) connects directly to mongo:27017 with mongosh and reads or rewrites the users collection without credentials.
assumptions: The mongo:4.4 container is started with its default configuration, which has no authentication enabled when no root credentials are supplied.
threats.impactReason: Unauthenticated database access allows full read and modification of every collection, including stored credentials.
threats.likelihoodReason: The port is not published to the host, so the attacker first needs code execution or SSRF inside the compose network, but any foothold gives immediate full access.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection used by the web service.
steps: Add MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME and MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD (from a secrets file, not literals) to the mongo service in docker-compose.yml.
Change MONGODB_URI at docker-compose.yml:8 to include the credentials and an authSource, and enable TLS on the mongod container.
Keep 27017 on `expose` only and add a dedicated network so other containers cannot reach it.

threats.title: Outdated mongodb 2.x driver pinned in package.json
threats.asset: the nodegoat MongoDB database contents
threats.attackScenario: package.json:18 pins "mongodb": "^2.1.18", a driver line that is end-of-life and whose BSON/query serialisation path predates fixes for prototype-pollution and injection issues, so an attacker who can influence a query object passed to collection.find() in the application reaches driver behaviour that the maintained 4.x/5.x line no longer exhibits.
assumptions: The deployed image installs the 2.x driver resolved by the ^2.1.18 range rather than an overridden newer version.
threats.impactReason: Driver-level weaknesses affect every query issued to the nodegoat database but require application-level reachability to exploit.
threats.likelihoodReason: The dependency is declared and unmaintained; exploitation still depends on an application query path accepting attacker-shaped objects.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade the mongodb driver to a supported major version.
steps: Raise "mongodb" in package.json:18 to a currently supported major release and adapt the connection code in server.js to the new MongoClient API.
Add an audit step (npm audit) to the existing scripts block so future advisories on the driver surface in CI.

threats.title: web container startup loop re-runs db-reset.js, allowing destructive restart-driven data loss
threats.asset: persisted nodegoat collections (users, allocations)
threats.attackScenario: The command at docker-compose.yml:9 runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js && npm start` inside an `until ... do sleep 2; done` loop, so an attacker who can crash the Node process on port 4000 causes the container command to loop and re-execute db-reset.js, wiping and reseeding the nodegoat database and destroying stored records.
assumptions: The container or orchestrator restarts the web service after a process crash.
artifacts/db-reset.js drops and reseeds collections rather than seeding only when empty.
threats.impactReason: A reset destroys all stored application data in the nodegoat database.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the attacker to first crash or restart the web process, which is an extra step beyond reaching port 4000.

mitigation.summary: Separate the seeding step from the application start command.
steps: Remove `node artifacts/db-reset.js` from the web service command in docker-compose.yml and run it as a one-off profile or init container.
Guard artifacts/db-reset.js so it refuses to run unless NODE_ENV is test or development.

threats.title: Seeder and DAO traffic to MongoDB travels unauthenticated and unencrypted over the compose network
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords, SSN and bank account details stored in the nodegoat users collection
threats.attackScenario: The connection string used by the seeder and all DAOs is `mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat` (docker-compose.yml:8, defaulted again in config/env/all.js:3) with no credentials, no authSource and no tls option, so any process or container that can reach port 27017 on the shared network connects as an anonymous client, reads the users collection written by artifacts/db-reset.js and app/data/profile-dao.js, and overwrites the admin document to set `isAdmin: true` on an account it controls.
assumptions: Another container or host process shares the network segment with the mongo service.
The application connects to MongoDB without authentication or with excessive privileges, as shown in the default docker-compose configuration.
The mongo:4.4 container is started without --auth and without TLS, as the credential-free URI implies.
threats.impactReason: Direct read/write on the users collection yields plaintext passwords, SSN and bank routing fields and permits privilege escalation to admin.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network position on the compose/orchestrator network rather than internet reachability, but no authentication step stands in the way once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authenticated, TLS-protected MongoDB connections for the seeder and application.
steps: Start the mongo service in docker-compose.yml with --auth and create a least-privilege application user scoped to the nodegoat database.
Change MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml:8 and the fallback in config/env/all.js:3 to include those credentials plus tls=true, and supply them from secrets rather than literals.
Remove the `expose: 27017` reachability for any service that does not need it and verify artifacts/db-reset.js fails closed when authentication is rejected.

threats.title: Seeder writes fixed default admin and user accounts with known credentials into the users collection
threats.asset: seeded default account credentials (the `admin` account in the users collection)
threats.attackScenario: artifacts/db-reset.js:12-37 inserts the fixed documents `userName: "admin"` with `isAdmin: true` and `user1`/`user2` with literal passwords taken from source, so once the seeder has run an attacker who reads this public repository signs in at the login page as `admin` with the documented fixture password and gains administrative access to every profile, allocation and benefits record.
assumptions: The literal password values stored in artifacts/db-reset.js are the same values accepted at login, i.e. the fixtures are not rotated after deployment.
threats.impactReason: A known-password admin account exposes all user profiles including SSN and bank details, plus benefits modification.
threats.likelihoodReason: The credentials are published in the repository and the seeder runs automatically at container start, so only reaching the login page is required.

mitigation.summary: Stop seeding fixed credentials into any non-development database.
steps: Read the seed account passwords from environment variables in artifacts/db-reset.js instead of the USERS_TO_INSERT literals, and abort if they are unset.
Hash seeded passwords with the bcrypt-nodejs dependency already used in app/data/user-dao.js before insertion.
Skip creation of the isAdmin account entirely unless an explicit development flag is set.

threats.title: Startup seeder drops every collection, destroying live user data on each container start
threats.asset: stored user accounts, allocations, contributions and memo records in the nodegoat MongoDB database
threats.attackScenario: The web service's command in docker-compose.yml:9 runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js` before `npm start`, and the script calls db.dropCollection (artifacts/db-reset.js:39-48) unconditionally, so anyone who can force a container restart (for example by crashing the Node process or triggering an orchestrator redeploy) wipes the users, allocations, contributions and memos collections and replaces them with the three fixed fixture accounts.
assumptions: The same compose/postdeploy startup command is used outside local development, so the seeder runs against a database holding real records.
threats.impactReason: All persisted application data, including profile SSN/bank fields and memos, is irrecoverably dropped and replaced by fixtures.
threats.likelihoodReason: No attacker credentials are needed beyond causing a restart, and ordinary operational restarts trigger it automatically.

mitigation.summary: Make seeding explicit and non-destructive outside development.
steps: Remove `node artifacts/db-reset.js` from the container command in docker-compose.yml:9 and from the `postdeploy` script in app.json:13, leaving seeding to the manual `npm run db:seed` path.
Guard the dropCollection loop in artifacts/db-reset.js so it exits immediately unless NODE_ENV is development or an explicit ALLOW_DB_RESET flag is set.
Have the script refuse to run when the users collection already contains documents that are not the fixture ids 1-3.

threats.title: Seeder leaves no attributable record of who reset and reseeded the database
threats.asset: audit trail for destructive database reset operations
threats.attackScenario: artifacts/db-reset.js reports its actions only with console.log to stdout (lines 43, 57-58) and records no operator identity, timestamp or prior row counts, so a person who runs `npm run db:seed` to wipe the users and memos collections and restore the fixture admin account can later deny doing so, and investigators cannot tell a deliberate reset from an automatic container restart.
assumptions: Container stdout is not shipped to a tamper-resistant log store that retains who invoked the seeder.
threats.impactReason: Loss of all application data cannot be attributed, hampering incident response and insider-abuse investigation.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires shell or deploy access to the container, but every run of the script already produces this gap by default.

mitigation.summary: Emit an attributable, durable audit record for each seeder run.
steps: Log the invoking user, NODE_ENV, target database URI host and pre-drop document counts in artifacts/db-reset.js before calling tryDropCollection.
Write that record to an append-only collection or external log sink rather than only stdout.

threats.title: Unauthenticated MongoDB endpoint lets an attacker on the network starve the seeder and application of the database
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat MongoDB database for the seeder and all DAO queries
threats.attackScenario: Because port 27017 is exposed on the compose network with a credential-free URI (docker-compose.yml:8, docker-compose.yml:16-17), an attacker with a foothold on that network opens unlimited anonymous connections or issues large unindexed find operations against the users and memos collections until the web container's startup command at docker-compose.yml:9 can no longer complete `node artifacts/db-reset.js` and the service loops on the `until nc -z` retry.
assumptions: The application connects to MongoDB without authentication or with excessive privileges, as shown in the default docker-compose configuration.
The mongo container runs without authentication or connection limits, so anonymous clients can open arbitrary numbers of sessions.
threats.impactReason: The application cannot start or serve any route while the database is saturated, though no data is disclosed or altered.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs an existing presence on the internal network; the database is not directly published to the internet by this compose file. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Authenticate and rate-limit database access and restrict network reachability.
steps: Enable MongoDB authentication and set maxIncomingConnections in the mongo service configuration in docker-compose.yml.
Place the mongo service on a dedicated internal network that only the web service joins.
Add a bounded retry and failure exit to the startup command so the web container reports a clear failure instead of looping indefinitely.

threats.title: web container publishes port 4000 on all host interfaces with no resource limits
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat web application
threats.attackScenario: docker-compose.yml:10-11 maps "4000:4000" without a host-interface prefix and the web service declares no cpus, mem_limit or restart policy, so an attacker on the same network as the host opens thousands of concurrent connections to http://host:4000 and exhausts the container's memory and event loop, taking the application offline.
assumptions: No reverse proxy, firewall or rate limiter sits in front of the published port in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: The single web container serves all traffic, so exhausting it is a full outage of the application.
threats.likelihoodReason: The bind is on all interfaces and needs no credentials, but the attacker must have network reach to the host.

mitigation.summary: Bind the published port to localhost behind a proxy and add container resource limits.
steps: Change the ports entry in docker-compose.yml to "127.0.0.1:4000:4000" and terminate public traffic at a reverse proxy that applies rate limiting.
Add mem_limit and cpus (or deploy.resources.limits) to the web service in docker-compose.yml.

threats.title: Container image built on end-of-life node:12-alpine base carrying unpatched CVEs
threats.asset: the running application container and the code and data it serves on port 4000
threats.attackScenario: The Dockerfile pins FROM node:12-alpine at lines 1 and 7, an end-of-life Node.js and Alpine base that no longer receives security updates, so an attacker who reaches the service exposed on port 4000 can drive a known unpatched Node 12 / OpenSSL / musl vulnerability in the base layer to crash or execute code inside the container.
assumptions: The image is rebuilt and deployed as written, without an external base-image patching or rebasing step.
threats.impactReason: A flaw in the base runtime affects the whole application process and any secrets or data it holds.
threats.likelihoodReason: Node 12 is EOL with publicly catalogued CVEs, but exploitation still requires a reachable vulnerable code path on port 4000.

mitigation.summary: Move the image to a currently supported, digest-pinned Node LTS base and scan it in CI.
steps: Change both `FROM node:12-alpine` lines in Dockerfile to a supported LTS tag (for example node:22-alpine) pinned by image digest.
Add a container image scan step to the existing GitHub Actions workflows so base-image CVEs fail the build.
Re-run the test matrix against the new Node version before shipping.

threats.title: Production hardening of the app directory is left commented out in the Dockerfile
threats.asset: application source and node_modules inside the container image
threats.attackScenario: Dockerfile line 15 leaves the `chown -R`/`chmod -R g-s,o-rx`/`chmod -R o-wrx` hardening commented out and only performs `COPY --chown=node . $WORKDIR`, so any process or injected code running as the `node` user in the container on port 4000 can overwrite files such as node_modules or application sources and have the tampered code execute on the next require or restart.
assumptions: The image is built as committed, with line 15 still commented, for production deployments.
threats.impactReason: Writable application code inside the container allows persistence and code modification after an initial foothold.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an existing code-execution or file-write foothold in the container; it is a post-exploitation amplifier rather than an entry point.

mitigation.summary: Apply the hardening that is currently commented out and make the application directory read-only to the runtime user.
steps: Uncomment and adapt the chown/chmod line at Dockerfile:15 so application files are owned by root and only readable by the `node` user.
Copy source with `COPY --chown=root:node` and drop write permission on $WORKDIR and node_modules.
Run the container with a read-only root filesystem and an explicit writable tmpfs for any scratch paths.

threats.title: E2E workflow triggers on pull_request with unpinned third-party actions and a shared cache
threats.asset: CI build outputs and the cached ~/.npm and ~/.cache contents reused by other workflow runs
threats.attackScenario: .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml runs on every `push` and `pull_request` and pulls actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-node@v1 and actions/cache@v2 by mutable tag rather than commit SHA, so an attacker who compromises or retags one of those action repositories — or who opens a fork pull request that poisons the `${{ runner.os }}-node...-E2E-...` npm cache entry during `npm ci` — gets attacker-controlled code executed in the e2e-test job and persisted into the cache consumed by later runs.
assumptions: The repository allows workflows to run on pull requests from forks without manual approval.
threats.impactReason: Code execution in CI can tamper with test results and poison the shared dependency cache used by subsequent builds; credentials are limited because persist-credentials is false.
threats.likelihoodReason: The workflow is triggered by any push or pull request, and mutable action tags plus shared caches are a routinely exercised supply-chain path.

mitigation.summary: Pin every third-party action to a full commit SHA and isolate caches for untrusted pull requests.
